Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei arrives near the White House for a meeting with President Donald Trump, Washington, DC, 29 September 2026 On October 14, Anthropic told potential investors that its third-quarter 2026 revenue reached $16.8 billion. The company also reported an adjusted profit for that period. Moreover, the company shared these figures at an investor event held at its San Francisco headquarters, just weeks before its planned stock market debut. The Financial Times first reported the numbers, and soon after, a Reuters report citing two attendees and a Bloomberg story citing people familiar with the matter gave the same revenue figure. Anthropic has not published the results, and it declined to comment to Bloomberg. The $16.8bn covers revenue earned in the quarter itself, so it differs from the annualised run rates often quoted for AI companies. According to Reuters, revenue was about $11.6bn in the second quarter and $4.7bn in the first, which puts the latest rise at about 45%. That second-quarter number is close to the earlier figure of more than $11.5bn in revenue that Anthropic shared with investors in August. At the time, the company also said its adjusted operating income was positive. None of the reports say which costs the adjusted measure leaves out, and no profit figure was given. However, Anthropic also told investors it was cash-flow positive in the quarter, the FT reported. The latest results follow a loss-making 2025, as last year, Anthropic’s revenue rose to nearly $4.6bn, while its operating loss topped $8bn. That loss figure excludes write-downs of liabilities linked mostly to earlier fundraising. Chief executive Dario Amodei and chief financial officer Krishna Rao both met investors at the event, according to Reuters. Those who went left upbeat about growth and the path to profit, the news agency reported. Meanwhile, the listing’s timing has shifted more than once. Anthropic had been expected to list in October, before the midterms. Bloomberg now reports that formal marketing could start as early as the week of November 9, with trading to begin before Thanksgiving on November 26. Bloomberg added that the plans remain fluid and the dates could change. Some prospective investors put a fair valuation for Anthropic at between $1.8tn and $2tn, the outlet reported, and the deal could match SpaceX’s record listing in size. Senior Consumer Insights Editor Senior Consumer Insights Editor  				Edited by Jon Skillings  October 15, 2026, 4:30 pm ET Google’s Universal Cart is rolling out across search and the Gemini app in the US, just ahead of Black Friday and the holiday shopping season.  Think less browser extension, more a way to shop within Google.  The Universal Cart is an AI-powered shopping tool that helps you stay on top of products you’re considering buying from a variety of retailers you encounter on Google. If you want to continue shopping later, Google will save your products and progress so you can pick up where you left off. The cart will refresh listings for over 60 billion products to keep an eye on price changes and low-stock alerts in Google’s Shopping Graph. More from CNET It can also alert you to price drops and when an item is back in stock.  Once you’ve narrowed your purchase, the Universal Cart — built on Google Wallet — can help you find promotional savings and choose which credit card reaps the most rewards. When you’re ready to buy, Google uses the Universal Commerce Protocol for checkout, and you can make purchases from your cart using Google Pay. Or you can move the items from Google to the merchant cart to finish your purchase. Your purchase confirmations and customer support will still come from the retailer.  However, there are some caveats. You’ll need to start through Google to shop, not the merchant’s website. It’s not quite a browser extension to add a button to every website you visit.  Meanwhile, Meta is touting the shopping capabilities of its newly introduced Muse AI agent. Google previewed the Universal Cart in May at its I/O developer forum.    		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

Author of the First Trade newsletter The stock market has spent much of 2026 being pushed around by two enormous forces: the Iran-war energy shock and the global AI buildout. Wednesday's inflation report suggests the broader economy is being pulled along by those same drivers — to the detriment of the everyday consumer. The headline was a hotter-than-expected CPI reading.  And the surprise wasn't just energy. Both headline and core CPI beat forecasts. That double upside surprise makes it harder to write the report off as simply another bad month at the gas pump. Speaking of which, gasoline was once again a clear pain point, jumping 9.1% from August to September and accounting for more than half of the index's overall increase. Then, buried further down the CPI table was an outsized 9.7% year-over-year spike in computers, peripherals, and smart-home assistants — the category most closely linked to the AI buildout. Put those together and you get a pretty good snapshot of the US economy in 2026: The price of getting around is dictated by geopolitics, while the price of plugging in is increasingly being shaped by the AI arms race. Investors have had to care about a relatively short list of things this year: oil, the handful of companies spending fortunes on data centers, and the exclusive club of firms supplying the chips, power, and equipment. This week's CPI report is a good reminder that those forces don't just stay in the stock market. Gasoline is the immediate problem. It's visible, politically charged, and can work its way into the cost of flying, shipping, manufacturing, and eventually plenty of other things. Energy costs were up more than 20% year-over-year last month. AI-linked consumer tech is a different kind of warning. It's not large enough to move the inflation needle on its own, and smartphones are actually getting cheaper. But computers are getting more expensive, challenging one of tech's classic consumer promises: that the gadgets of tomorrow will be better — and cheaper — than the ones we have today. That's what makes the recent shift so striking. For most of the time since BLS began tracking the category in 2005, computer products were deflationary. Blame the global memory-chip shortage for a big part of this year's spike into inflationary territory. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. When it comes to addressing the US inflation problem, the Fed's toolkit is pretty limited. It can raise rates, but it can't create another barrel of oil, end a war, or make more memory chips. But the central bank can't just turn a blind eye either. Especially when you consider that core CPI, which doesn't include energy, was still up 2.6% year-over-year in September. The Fed's job is not to solve the source of the inflation problem — it's to keep those pressures from spreading into wages and services. It's an awkward job in an economy where the sources of inflation are unusually hard to cool. A rate hike could further squeeze shoppers, homebuyers, and businesses. It would do far less to change the global oil supply or the spending plans of tech giants. That's the 2026 policy trap. In order to contain price pressures, the Fed may have to slow parts of the economy unrelated to drilling and building data centers. Oil prices have fallen from wartime peaks, but a broader transportation crisis in the crude market suggests it may not matter so far as preventing further pain for consumers.   Energy costs have been top of mind for investors for most of this year as the war has dragged on. Brent crude, the international benchmark, has seesawed recently, trading around $105 a barrel this week as traders weighed supply disruptions alongside the outlook for a resolution to the war.  But it's no longer an oil supply shortage energy experts are worried about — it's a shipping crisis that has drawn more attention recently, analysts watching the crude market say. Shipping costs are thought to be secondary to the price of oil when it comes to energy costs, but that's changed recently as tanker rates and diesel prices have skyrocketed, reflecting how the market is pricing in a higher premium for transporting oil out of the Middle East, as well as reduced refining capacity to produce fuel.  For consumers, it's fundamentally changed the equation for the cost of supplying oil — meaning energy costs could stay high even if oil prices cooled from their current levels, energy experts say. Rates for Very Large Crude Carriers, a type of large tanker frequently used in the Persian Gulf, have more than quadrupled in the past year, rising from about $50,000 a day in late 2025 to over $200,000 a day in October, according to the shipping intelligence site Fearnpulse. The cost of VLCC trips from the Persian Gulf to the Far East has risen from under $2 per barrel to over $30 per barrel year-to-date, according to a separate estimate from BCA Research. Diesel, a refined oil product that fuels ships and other modes of transportation, has also exacerbated the situation. Diesel prices remain near a record high, clocking in at around $6.29 a gallon this week, AAA data shows. Some ships traveling through the Middle East are also being forced to make a longer voyage, given the blockade of the Bab-el Mandeb Strait, BCA said. Recent attacks, meanwhile, have reduced the world's supply of oil tankers that are in working condition. The world has lost around 20 oil tankers in the last 2 weeks, according to one estimate from HFI Research, a contrarian energy research firm. "The recovery in Middle Eastern crude exports has come at the price of a surge in transportation costs, which is creating major dislocations in global crude markets," BCA Research wrote in a client note. "While the surge in dark transits through the Strait of Hormuz has eased tightness in global crude supplies, it is too early to declare the all-clear for oil markets," the firm said of how transportation issues could override relief from increased exports. Oil flows coming out of the Gulf have been better than expected, reaching around 81% of their pre-war norms during the month of September, according to Kpler data. Energy inflation, though, accelerated significantly in the month of September, rising 5.2% over the last month, per the latest consumer price index. The surge in transportation costs means another $35-$40 should be factored into the price for each barrel of oil, according to Helima Croft, the global head of commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets. She pointed to how Trafigura's recent charter of the Alexandros, one large oil tanker set to travel from the US Gulf Coast to China, recently rose to $76 million, up from the normal rate of $7 million to $10 million, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC this month. "We're in a transportation crisis," Croft said, speaking to CNBC on the supply and price pressures in the oil market. "The shortage is really now coming to ships, coming to cruise that will move this product to refineries." Shipping challenges also directly affect the price of oil, pushing up energy costs. Last month, Kpler flagged the possibility that crude could rise as high as $150 a barrel, pointing to pressures stemming from the diesel market and disrupted flows in the Red Sea and in the Strait of Hormuz. HFI Research floated the possibility that Brent crude could rise as high as $135 a barrel by early November, citing limited tanker supply and higher rates as factors putting upward pressure on prices. "If the current escalation continues (multiple tankers attacked daily) and the Oman Lane flow slowdown persists, I see Brent reaching $133 to $135," HFI wrote in a recent note. If you're hoping to get an early-career job in the age of AI, get ready to pick up the hard hat, scrubs, or chalk. Recent graduates are entering a job market where entry-level work is increasingly being reshaped by AI models, but not all fields may be equally exposed. Business Insider analyzed data from a September working paper by US Census Bureau researchers that estimates the extent to which different fields of study are exposed to AI. The paper evaluates exposure by assessing whether GPT-4 could substantially reduce the time required to complete tasks in jobs that young graduates in each field typically enter. Some of the most exposed fields, according to the working paper, include computer-focused fields such as computer science, computer engineering, and computer programming, as well as information sciences. Statistics, applied mathematics, electrical engineering, actuarial science, and journalism also ranked among the highest-exposure fields. The study found that graduates in the highest-exposure fields were 5 percentage points less likely to be employed in the quarter after graduation and had 13% lower initial full-quarter earnings than graduates in less-exposed fields after ChatGPT became widely available in 2022. On the other hand, fields like teaching, medical assisting, and nutrition were found to be among the least exposed to AI. For this ranking, Business Insider looked at the fields in the paper's three lowest-exposure deciles and combined closely related specialties to rank the 25 least-exposed general career paths. While looking at job exposure to AI can help draw a picture of what jobs may be more vulnerable, this ranking isn't definitive, and the study reflects only GPT-4's ability to speed up job tasks. See what college majors might be safest from AI in the future. This broad science degree combines biology, chemistry, physics, math, and environmental science. Graduates often work as lab or research assistants, technicians, science educators, or specialists. Many also use it as preparation for various health professions education. The work of dietitians and nutritionists often involves tailoring advice to each patient's health and circumstances, such as culture, budget, and lifestyle. Graduates also often go on to work as public health specialists or health educators. Criminology experts often work in community-focused areas like law enforcement, corrections, crime analysis, or victim services. Their work often involves interpreting behavior and evidence, making difficult judgment calls with legal and community safety consequences. Some may say AI art will replace human artists, but we probably won't see an Oscar-winning AI model for a while. Performance and studio artists, such as performers, musicians, actors, painters, sculptors, and designers, may be among the least replaceable professionals in the age of AI, as their work showcases human creativity, performance, and collaboration. The core of subjects like philosophy and literature is often human by design. Liberal arts graduates often apply their studies and skills to analyzing, expressing, and adapting ideas in areas such as law, communications, nonprofit work, public service, research, education, and business. Physiology graduates study the human body's systems and often go on to work in clinical research, laboratory work, health education, or other health professions. Their work often involves supporting patient care and interpreting biological findings. Graduates in family and consumer sciences help people make better decisions about relationships, finances, and family well-being; they often work in areas like human development, family services, consumer education, and community programs. Social work and human services graduates often help people navigate crises, connect with benefits, access adequate care, and build support networks. They also often deal with uniquely complex circumstances that require specialized judgment and trust. Health sciences and pre-health programs prepare students for careers in medicine, dentistry, physician-assistant studies, public health, clinical research, or patient support. Graduates often work directly with patients, healthcare systems, and care teams. Speech therapists and communication disorder majors study how speech develops in humans and how to address various challenges affecting communication. Their work often involves assessing and treating different conditions in speech, hearing, language, and communication through individualized patient care. Forestry, natural resource management, and ecology majors often work as foresters, conservation scientists, environmental planners, land managers, or wildlife technicians. Their work often involves monitoring ecosystems and managing land based on ground conditions. So far, AI cannot save anyone from a burning house. Graduates in criminal justice and fire protection work in highly physically demanding fields that require a high level of situational awareness and preparedness, such as first responders, fire services, policing and corrections, and public safety administration. Specialists in transportation and logistics are the human motor behind the supply chain. They often work in freight operations, warehousing, dispatching, transportation, and fleet management. Their work involves coordinating transportation routes and schedules as well as managing disruptions. Graduates of secondary and teacher education programs are the backbone of high school curricula and often go on to teach in subjects such as math, science, English, social studies, art, and music. Beyond level- and subject-specific teaching, general education studies are also a solid path for those looking to enter education, which is overall one of the safest fields in terms of exposure to AI. Graduates' work often focuses on teaching, curriculum development, and instructional support. Graduates from these programs often go on to work as physical education teachers, coaches, fitness professionals, or youth program leaders. Graduates from plant sciences and agronomy programs often use their knowledge and skills to assess soil health, manage pests, maximize yields, and make weather-based decisions while working with crops, farms, and greenhouses for agricultural companies. Graduates in animal sciences and zoology often work in animal care, zoos, conservation, research, wildlife biology, and agriculture. Their work often involves working directly with animals to study their health, behavior, habitats, and ecosystems. Nursing provides uniquely human patient care that AI can't replicate yet. Their work often involves applying clinical judgment and providing hands-on care, including administering medication, monitoring patient symptoms, and collaborating with medical teams. Programs in physical and occupational therapy often lead to careers focused on patient rehabilitation, with high demand for hands-on assessment and the development of tailored recovery plans. Special education teachers support students with disabilities in achieving educational goals by adapting instruction, developing individualized plans, and working closely with students, families, and specialists to build academic and life skills. This work demands patience, knowledge, and interpersonal skills from graduates. Graduates working with medical laboratories and clinical technologies test blood, tissue, and other patient samples. In doing so, they help doctors diagnose and treat illness. These trained professionals ensure reliable results and troubleshoot problems with automated equipment. The safest category of teachers in terms of AI exposure is those who work directly with a school's youngest students. Teachers in elementary and early-childhood education are key to helping children achieve foundational learning and social development. Their work often involves managing young classrooms, working closely with parents, and developing lesson plans for different student needs. AI is not replacing school principals anytime soon. Graduates of educational administration and leadership often go on to work as school principals, district administrators, and instructional leaders after gaining classroom experience and other credentials. Their work involves managing staff, responding to parents' needs, setting school- or district-wide priorities, and making community-shaping decisions. Even high-tech clinics need someone assisting at a patient's bedside. Medical assisting is the safest field in terms of AI exposure, according to the US Census Bureau working paper.  Graduates in the field often work on patient intake, taking vital signs, and handling administrative tasks such as updating medical histories and scheduling future care. While AI might streamline the paperwork side of medical care, the industry still depends on direct patient contact to keep a clinic running. No comments right now, check back later. Netflix has hired a new content chief after a stock slump and struggles to grow its viewership. Peter Rice, a former Fox and Disney executive, will oversee Netflix's $20 billion budget for movies and shows starting on October 26, the company announced on Thursday. Rice will replace Bela Bajaria, who's leaving the company after almost a decade. Bajaria took the top content job in 2023 and memorably described the ideal Netflix show as a "gourmet cheeseburger." The exec shake-up came a day after the streaming giant laid off about 1,000 employees, its biggest round of layoffs in four years. Netflix has had a tough year. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos said at a Bloomberg media event last month that Netflix is "not growing as fast as I want us to, and we're working on making that move faster." Shares are down nearly 40% in the past 12 months as investors increasingly worry about slower viewership growth and the company's long-term direction. Netflix's attempt to buy Warner Bros. — which was ultimately stymied by David Ellison's Paramount — soured the Wall Street narrative about the company's future. Rice was previously the head of Disney's TV arm, where he ran Hulu and networks like ABC, Disney Channel, and FX. He was fired from the Mouse House in 2022 by former Disney CEO Bob Chapek and replaced by Dana Walden, who's now Disney's creative chief. "Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry," Sarandos said in a statement. The co-CEO added that Rice's "business acumen is sharp, his talent relationships are exceptionally strong, and his experience across TV and film is deep and broad." Bajaria "led enormous changes at Netflix," Sarandos said, crediting her for helping the streamer broaden its content mix to live events and sports. Under Bajaria, Netflix had hits like "KPop Demon Hunters" — its biggest movie ever — as well as breakout shows like "Wednesday" and Emmy Award winner "Adolescence." However, Netflix's engagement growth was only 2% in the first half of 2026, and the company has faced increased competition from free streamers like YouTube and Tubi. YouTube is now well ahead of Netflix as the most-watched service on US TV screens. Netflix, which had more than 325 million subscribers as of its last disclosure in January, remains the clear leader among paid streaming services. That said, Rice will have to figure out the right content mix to fend off both its Hollywood rivals and social-media competitors like Instagram and TikTok. No comments right now, check back later. Tesla CEO Elon Musk is about to pull the wraps off the second-generation Roadster — again. It's been nine years since Elon Musk said it would revive the Roadster. Would-be buyers chomped at the bit to grab the two-door, 600-mile-range, high-powered electric car way back in November 2017. They paid either $50,000 to reserve a spot in the car's queue or $250,000 to buy a Founders Series upfront. Roughly nine years later, the car still hasn't entered production. That could change soon, as Tesla is about to unveil the car — now apparently with cold-gas thrusters that might allow it to temporarily hover — on Thursday night. That raised an expensive question: What if early Roadster buyers had put that money into Tesla stock instead? So we did some back-of-the-napkin math to figure it out. Tesla shares closed at about $21 on November 17, 2017, the first trading day after Musk unveiled the car. At roughly $360 in mid-October 2026, a $50,000 investment made in 2017 would now be worth between $850,000 and $900,000. That's a gain of more than $800,000, before taxes and trading fees. A buyer who put down the full $250,000 for a limited Founders Series Roadster would be sitting on roughly $4.3 million in Tesla stock today, a gain of about $4 million. The long wait for the Roadster's deliveries has not gone unnoticed by Musk. During an October 2024 earnings call, he thanked the vehicle's "long-suffering" deposit holders, while saying the car company had focused heavily on its autonomy and robotics ambitions. In the 8-bit home computer boom of the early 1980s, Sir Clive Sinclair’s machines were always among the cheapest on the market, often packing a surprising level of sophistication in their limited hardware. If there was one component that was key to their success it was the Ferranti ULA, or Uncommitted Logic Array, a clever way to make an ASIC from a chip containing a library of logic parts ready made. The Sinclair ULAs have been reverse engineered, but their full details have remained a mystery. Until now it seems, because here’s [Happy Little Diodes] with a treasure trove of original Ferranti design documents covering all the Sinclair parts. The documents were picked up on eBay, and contain folders with printouts, engineering drawings, and hand written design notes. They cover the full range of Sinclair products of the era, including the ZX81 and Spectrum, the ZX printer, the Microdrive, the Spectrum Interface 1, and even the curious little flat screen TV. Oddly the IP is now held by the satellite broadcaster Sky as the holder of Amstrad’s portfolio, but fortunately Sky have recognised their historical importance and allowed their sharing with minimal changes. They’re all catalogued with download links in a Google spreadsheet, so dig in and see what you can find. Of particular interest are the ULAs that haven’t been reverse engineered yet, and the subtle differences between different versions of the same ULA as the engineers tried to fix bugs. The video is below the break. If you’re curious about the ULA and Ferranti, we linked to a period film about it.   That’s awesome! Btw, there’s also an excellent book (which I just happen to have!) called “The ZX Spectrum ULA: How to Design a Microcomputer” by Chris Smith. If you’re a fan of vintage machines, you should take a sneak peek. Just saying. Please be kind and respectful to help make the comments section excellent. Over 20 years of combined experience and the latest in technology, AI,… Hacksaw Group has launched a B2B prediction-market platform for operators, entering a sector where annual global trading volume could reach about $1 trillion by 2030, according to an estimate cited in the company’s announcement. The Stockholm-listed technology and game developer says the platform will let operators offer peer-to-peer prediction markets using Hacksaw’s technology, distribution network and operator relationships. The company says Bernstein estimated the market’s annual volume could reach that level as adoption expands; it is not a forecast of Hacksaw’s own business. The platform is designed to spare operators from building and maintaining the underlying technology themselves. They can offer prediction-market experiences within their own businesses while retaining their brands, customer relationships and user experiences, according to the Hacksaw announcement. Hacksaw says its connected volume framework is intended to pool peer-to-peer participation across its operator network, giving participating businesses access to broader capacity from launch. The company also says it developed the platform within its existing cost base. The announcement does not specify operator customers, trading volumes, revenue or a rollout schedule. The Malta Gaming Authority has approved an extension of Hacksaw’s existing B2B Critical Gaming Supply License to include Type 3 Gaming Services, alongside its existing Type 1 authorization. Hacksaw says the extension authorizes B2B peer-to-peer prediction-market services under Malta’s regulatory framework; it does not establish where or when individual operators will offer the product. “Prediction markets represent a compelling new opportunity at the intersection of technology, entertainment and market participation,” said Ana Vrabic Verdir, Group CEO of Hacksaw Group. Louis, Otis and Ben all have differing opinions on whether teens should use protein powder Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum.  "I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!", he says, claiming it would make him "fitter and bigger" and that his male friends use it. In recent years, there's been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein", including milk, yoghurt, breads, cereals, bars and powders. Social media is flooded with adverts for various supplements, including protein powder.  As a health journalist, I'm sceptical and think at Ben's age he must be getting enough protein through his diet. So, do experts think it's safe for pre-teens and teenagers or is a big, juicy steak just as good? In recent years, there has been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein"... ... however, protein is found in lots of everyday foods, including meat, fish, eggs, dairy, bread, grains and pulses My sport-obsessed son, who already eats a healthy balanced diet, asks me about protein powder on a regular basis. His friend Louis, 12, has been using protein powder once or twice a week for nearly a year, after a workout and on top of whole foods. His parents are aware of this. "I think it's helped, it gives me more energy and it's helped me grow, probably," he says. But Ben's other friend Otis, who is 13, is not keen on the idea and feels there is pressure on young people to take protein supplements. "They might just start using them without thinking about the consequences or what effects it may have on them." Proteins break down into amino acids that help the body grow and repair. But your body can't make all the amino acids it needs on its own, so you need to get more - known as essential amino acids - through your diet. For an adult with a healthy weight, the recommended daily amount of protein you should be eating is 0.75 grams per kg of body weight, according to the NHS. A good rule of thumb is that the amount of protein you have for each meal should fit into the palm of your hand. If you exercise a lot, and when you get older, you need more protein so you could have up to 2 grams per kg of body weight. But do teens really need it if they're eating well? This video can not be played Do you really need protein powder to build muscle? For teenage boys and girls "you can get all the protein that you need from food alone", says registered dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine. It is important that teenage girls, especially, get enough iron and calcium, so Ludlam-Raine says not to become overly focused on protein at the expense of other nutrients. Protein shakes, powders or bars can be useful for some, including high-level athletes and those who have certain allergies, but they should not replace a healthy diet. There can also be some unwanted side effects from using protein powders such as bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea. Those with pre-existing health conditions should not use it unless they have been told they can by their doctor. Ludlam-Raine points out that the protein powder market is not as tightly regulated as medicines. "Of course, you can get reputable companies who do third-party testing and make sure that what you see on the label is what is in the inside, but that's not always the case," she says. "And ultimately you can't just have a shake and your biceps grow." Some protein powders contain high amounts of added sugar, artificial ingredients, and hidden stimulants. Dr Ramnik Mathur is a consultant paediatrician from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Trust. He explains that we need micronutrients like zinc, calcium and magnesium, which are found in whole foods. So, if meals are replaced with protein shakes, those nutrients are lost. Experts suggest spreading out protein across the day and aiming for 20-25g per meal. If you're keen to up your intake, try some of these recipes. During puberty when children have growth spurts, they do need more protein because their body is growing rapidly, building new muscle and bone mass. But Mathur says there are risks to eating too much protein. "If you look at social media, they'll say you need to eat a lot of protein, but your body can handle only so much." He explains that if you eat too much, it has to be excreted by the kidneys and liver which can become overloaded. Mathur explains: "We had a child here at the hospital where I work - he was taking so much protein that his kidneys just stopped working and he actually passed away." The key takeaway from Mathur: "If a 12-year-old child is eating a healthy balanced diet then they shouldn't need any more protein." Ludlam-Raine's advice is to get teens to improve their diet first before taking any protein powder, especially regularly. If they still want to use it, speak to a registered dietitian or nutritionist first. Now off I go to tell my son the answer is still no - and the experts say the same. The king of streaming is shrinking parts of its kingdom. Netflix is cutting roughly 1,000 employees, or about 6% of its staff, in the streamer's largest round of layoffs since 2022. Product, tech, and HR teams are among the areas being hit. It comes amid a dark stretch for Netflix's stock, which is down almost 42% over the past year and nearly 25% in 2026. BI's Jame Faris broke down five key reasons why Netflix has been having such a tough time. But the layoffs didn't immediately ease investors' concerns. Netflix's stock price barely moved, finishing the day up 0.16%. BI's Peter Kafka does a good job of explaining why Netflix's problems won't be solved by job cuts. Netflix reports earnings on Tuesday, but the streamer's pain point isn't a secret: engagement. With roughly 325 million paid subscribers, Netflix's reach is still massive. But investors have been dogging Netflix about how long all those people are engaging with its shows. Things came to a head this summer during Netflix's second-quarter earnings. Following lukewarm results, Netflix said it wasn't going to release audience numbers as often. Holding back information from investors isn't typically a great sign. But there's an argument that focusing on the performance of Netflix's new, shiny shows is missing the point. The streamer's success often comes from older shows' massive tails. That still doesn't address the biggest risk to Netflix and other streamers. From TikTok and Instagram to YouTube and free TV, people have a lot of options. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. Here’s what building two companies, and scaling my app to a million downloads, taught me about execution. Copied to clipboard  		Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.	 Back in 1999, there was this company called Webvan. They had an idea for an online delivery service — something so routine for us now, but so revolutionary for that time. They raised over a billion dollars, went public and were bankrupt within two years. Why? Because a brilliant idea ≠ success. Sam Walton, who founded Walmart, did not invent the discount store. His idea wasn’t genius or novel, and he openly admitted to copying most of his best approaches from competitors. But he and his team executed better than anyone else, turning a copied idea into the largest retailer on Earth. “Ideas are easy. Execution is everything,” as John Doerr, the legendary VC behind Google and Amazon, once said. As a founder of a self-improvement app that reached over 1M app downloads in less than two years and helps over 400K users grow every month, I couldn’t agree more.  Despite RiseGuide being a completely unique product, we give all the credit to our ability to execute. Superior execution consistently outperforms a superior concept for a few reasons: While there is no guaranteed recipe for success, I can surely share what worked and continues working for us. Your execution can only be as good as the people behind it. A wrong hire is expensive — at least 30% of that person’s first-year pay, according to the US Department of Labor’s estimate, and on a small team, it lowers the standard for everyone and kills the culture. At RiseGuide, our best people come through headhunting and referrals, not inbound applications, because strong people are rarely out looking. We also don’t have HR. Each team has hiring managers who are experienced and understand business context — they own the hiring process.  However, their decision is not final. The person who needs to fill the seat will never be fully objective. Instead, we bring in one of the co-founders with nothing to gain or lose, so they can judge the candidate with a clear head and say “no” if the fit is wrong — even if the search has been going on for months. Once you have a star, give them room. Instead of drawing a perfect org chart and slotting people into boxes, we find strong people and shape the role around what they do best, so they can reach their full potential instead of shrinking to fit a job description. As Steve Jobs put it, “It doesn’t make sense to hire smart people and then tell them what to do; we hire smart people so they can tell us what to do.” For two peak seasons, I worked as a creative marketer alongside my team: I learned the tools and briefed our creatives. We call it All Hands, Hands On. We don’t have managers in a traditional sense — everyone gets their hands dirty. Such an approach not only helps managers understand the context and their team better, but also increases overall team morale: When people watch the bar being met by the person who set it, they trust their decision more and execute better. With Trible, the previous product I co-founded and later helped sell, the first version took about half a year, because instead of building it, we spent far too much time debating over go-to-market strategy, branding and org structure. So now, we move fast.  We launched RiseGuide in about three weeks after the Trible exit, and it took us less than two hours to decide on a brand name and buy the domain. Of course, this only applies to decisions you can reverse, which are most of them. But the few you truly can’t undo are the ones you better contemplate carefully. Many businesses run on the assumption that everything is a trade-off: quality or speed, growth or customer care. But we don’t accept that. We grow marketing spend without giving up returns, move fast without cutting quality and push revenue without hurting retention. Good enough is never enough. At the same time, “no trade-offs” is not the same as perfectionism. There is a well-known Pareto principle, which says that roughly 80% of the value comes from 20% of the effort. So, don’t spend 80% of your time on endless polish that steals focus from building something new. We’d much rather ship a good solution in a few weeks than a bigger one that takes a few months. Of course, ideas also matter. In the end, people love buying them. But if you want those people to stay with your product and outperform the competition, you need to execute faster and better than anyone on the market. I would not want you to read the practices in this article as some kind of formula, because they are not. This is what worked for us. There are many ways to build a good business and team culture, and the CEO’s real job is finding the one that suits you and the people around you. Back in 1999, there was this company called Webvan. Reporter 2 Reporter 2  				Edited by Corinne Reichert  October 15, 2026, 8:00 am ET Apple’s first swing in the foldables market, the iPhone Duo, has already made a huge splash before it’s even available to buy.  The foldables segment has been overrun by Android devices, and all eyes have been patiently waiting for Apple to make its move. And the Duo’s design confirms the popularity of Samsung’s Galaxy Fold 8 and Google’s original Pixel Fold: Shorter and wider seems to be the sweet spot, as opposed to the more traditional taller folding phone designs we see with something like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.  But this is Apple we’re talking about, and the iPhone Duo is more than just an iOS version of the Galaxy Fold and Pixel Fold — it has a lot going for it. We had a lot of things to say about it during our hands-on with the device, and while personally, it seems like the best foldable I’ll never buy, it certainly will be delivered into the pockets of some discerning customers who want the Apple level of polish (or who can’t stand green message bubbles). More from CNET So who needs the iPhone Duo? Who is it best suited to? We know that the latest iPhone 18 Pro Max is for photography enthusiasts and those who want the best battery ever in an iPhone, but the Duo doesn’t provide that. It’s an oddly-shaped but good-looking device that fills a new space in Apple’s lineup.  Is the iPhone Duo actually for anyone in particular? There are a few crowds that are more likely to gravitate toward this foldable over others. Your grandparents likely aren’t going to run out and grab the Duo, but here’s who likely will.  Read More: iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone Duo: Comparing Apple’s New Pro Phone Against Its First Foldable There are likely plenty of Apple fans who have been waiting for its first foldable, but a lot of people also likely won’t pick up a first-generation device, preferring to wait until the second or third version so that Apple works out any kinks. (On the other hand, Apple has patiently waited and watched the foldable market, so its first swing might not feel like a first-generation foldable full of finicky foibles at all. It’s probably going to be great.) But there will be some early adopters and tech enthusiasts who won’t care and plan to get this phone anyway. Power users and those looking essentially for a foldable iPad Mini are going to love the iPhone Duo. You’ll likely be able to resize apps side by side, similar to how you would on any iPad, making it a dream for those who want an iPad experience with an iPhone form factor that fits right in your pocket. Still, we’ll need to see just how well multiple apps work on the inner screen simultaneously. It might not be as elegant as you’d get on an iPad, but it’s close.  The other group that might really want to get their mitts on the Duo is the professional crowd. The larger inner screen makes way for easier work apps that would be more cumbersome than even the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Editing Excel or Google Sheets spreadsheets, Google and Word docs, checking emails and sending work chats will be a far smoother experience on the wider display. Throw in a wireless keyboard, and you might have a pocket iPad-like productivity suite of your dreams. Apple products are synonymous with style, and this is a crowd that will happily gravitate toward this phone.  The new “it” item will be in the pockets of celebrities and content creators who want to make sure they’re seen with Apple’s newest device. It’s also an expensive phone, like all foldables, making it a status symbol that maintains the cool and pretentious vibe that Apple products give off.  Avid readers may also want to pick up the iPhone Duo, since it’s virtually the perfect e-reader size. Not only that, but you’ll also get access to the App Store, which doesn’t limit you just to Amazon’s Kindle Store or e-reader apps.  That type of flexibility on top of the power of iOS and the A20 Pro chip makes this a killer Kindle or e-reader replacement. While it is very expensive to replace a Kindle, its style, form and functionality would make it a worthy consideration for some people. If your priorities are camera features, battery life and durability, your first choice shouldn’t be the iPhone Duo. What you’re looking for is the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It checks all of those boxes, and you shouldn’t be swayed by the novelty of the Duo.  It’s not that the Duo isn’t alluring, but it’s both nearly double the price of the latest iPhone 18 Pro handsets and likely significantly less durable. The iPhone Duo costs about as much as a new iPhone 18 Pro and an iPad combined.  Like most foldables, the iPhone Duo doesn’t ship with issues, just compromises. That’s something that really needs to be considered when making your purchasing decision. This device is a marvel of engineering, wrapped in luxurious style, but 90% of people spending money on new phones are not going to buy this one.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. Brian Moynihan, Bank of America’s chair and chief executive, in an official DHS portrait from 2022. Bank of America brought in about 1,000 outside contractors in the second quarter to repair software weaknesses exposed by AI models, chief executive Brian Moynihan said on 14 October. One of those models, he said, was Anthropic’s Mythos. Moynihan disclosed the figure in an interview with CNBC after the bank reported third-quarter results, and discussed it again on the earnings call. TNW has not independently verified the numbers. About 3,000 of the bank’s own staff were already assigned to the same work before the contractors joined, Moynihan told CNBC. According to his account, the weaknesses lay in the code used by both the bank and its outside vendors. Moynihan told analysts on the call that the quarter included “a couple hundred million dollars plus” in remediation costs. That sum covered two separate jobs: the Mythos work and repairs to the bank’s anti-money-laundering controls. He expects the Mythos share to shrink now that the extra workers are in place. The 1,000 contractors are “not in the headcount” because the bank hired them as consultants, Moynihan said. The compliance spending follows Treasury penalties of more than $1.21 billion announced on 13 October. Federal regulators said the bank had failed to report suspicious transactions worth $5 billion and to finish steps ordered in 2024. Revenue for the quarter rose about 3% to nearly $30 billion. Even so, adjusted earnings of $1.08 a share fell short of analyst forecasts, and the stock closed almost 5% lower. Anthropic made Mythos available in April to a small group of companies, banks, and government agencies through a programme called Project Glasswing. The aim was to let them find and patch flaws before attackers did. A month later, US regulators paused some cyber exams to give the largest banks time to fix what the model had found. Moynihan had signalled the scale of the task before. In July he told Bloomberg Television that the model meant a big change in the amount of work banks would have to do. Jamie Dimon, who runs JPMorgan Chase, said in May that his bank had hundreds of people on the job full-time. Pressure from supervisors is also rising. Regulators in the US and Europe are questioning banks about AI agents and cyber risks, and the European Central Bank wants plans against AI-enabled threats by the end of October. Edited by David Watsky  October 15, 2026, 10:18 am ET The universal push for better hydration has produced a seemingly endless supply of water bottles that promise to keep H2O cold for hours, days, even months. Admittedly, “months” is a stretch, but given recent advances in insulation technology, that milestone may not be far off. Fresh off Stanley’s early-2020s hype, a new water bottle contender, Coldest, piqued my interest with its bold, brazen name alone. The company’s line of bottles and tumblers, which come in a range of sizes, styles and limited-edition designs, was featured on ABC’s “Shark Tank” and promises to keep beverages cold for 36 hours.  Coldest also operates out of my hometown of Naples in Florida (which I didn’t realize until I researched it), and I welcome any opportunity to support a local small business. But did it ultimately live up to its hype, the thousands of positive reviews and the praise from national media outlets?  More from CNET For comparison, I grabbed my go-to $30 Owala water bottle and filled it with equal amounts of water (three cups) and ice (one cup). This model is a different size and shape than the 46-ounce Coldest, which means the liquid and ice were more condensed in the compartment. That said, despite the lack of error-free, controlled-environment analysis, the primary goal was to determine whether the Coldest water bottle lived up to its 36-hour promise.  After only a few hours, both water bottles delivered refreshing, ice-cold agua, with Owala consistently beating Coldest by a couple of degrees. Using a meat thermometer, here is a breakdown of the reading times and temperatures across 36 hours:  After 3 Hours After 7 Hours After 15 Hours After 18 Hours After 24 Hours After 36 Hours While water certainly remained cool after the experiment concluded, it was by no means teeth-chattering cold. Though I can hardly imagine anyone waiting this long to drink a beverage, it’s still worth noting since this is a major part of Coldest’s marketing claim.  Owala’s water bottle, though smaller in volume, yielded a consistently colder liquid, likely because of its smaller surface area and greater exposure to the stainless steel interior. But after 36 hours, both bottles tied in temperature, giving Coldest a slight edge because of its significantly larger size.  My feelings towards Coldest were essentially neutral. While I appreciate the company’s ability to retain a cult-like following with monthly limited-edition design drops, I didn’t feel its water-cooling technology was any more superior than the models I currently own (including the Owala).  It’s clear that this was introduced to disrupt Stanley’s virality and market share, though I’m not entirely sure if I’d cough up the cash to make it part of my must-have accessory rotation. I didn’t dislike it, by any means, and applaud the founders on their early success, but even loyalty points and an affiliate program wouldn’t incentivize consistent buys, despite my obsession with staying hydrated and color-coordinating my outfits.  Those who collect water bottles like Pokémon will certainly think otherwise, as the impressive range of designs can be exciting. They are one-of-a-kind, often glow in the dark, and reflect current seasons and holidays, which is undeniably adorable. If that’s your thing, then great. But if your main concern is quenching thirst, you’re likely thinking less about style and more about substance, so any popular drinking vessel will do.   		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. The “not carried” status on a product is different from simply being out of stock. When an item is out of stock, it just means the product is temporarily unavailable, but the retailer plans to restock once new inventory arrives from the manufacturer. In contrast, a "not carried" label implies the product is no longer part of the retailer's active catalog. Therefore, the retailer does not expect to restock the item. Custom GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards from Nvidia partners such as Asus, MSI, and Gigabyte are still listed on Micro Center’s website for now. However, a closer look shows these models are out of stock at all of the retailer’s physical locations. This widespread unavailability lends credence to the rumors that Nvidia has reportedly stopped producing the GeForce RTX 5090. The Asus GeForce RTX 5090 ROG Astral Edition 20 is the only GeForce RTX 5090 graphics card that remains in stock at most Micro Center stores nationwide. However, there is a catch. This particular model is only available as part of the exclusive Asus ROG 20th Anniversary Bundle priced at almost $11,000. I’ve noticed an interesting trend over the past few years in my work as corporate counsel for startups and founders: foreign entrepreneurs launching U.S. companies specifically to self-sponsor their visas. With traditional employment-based green cards bogged down by low quotas, processing backlogs and strict per-country limits, building a U.S. business has become an increasingly attractive visa strategy. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) updates and policy clarifications that better accommodate international founders have accelerated this trend.  An immigration lawyer determines which visa pathway is the best fit. But your chances of success at actually winning that self-sponsorship visa also hinge on how your company’s corporate governance is built. If it’s sloppy, no immigration attorney can save your application. That’s why you need corporate counsel at the table from day one.  Most founders get tripped up at the intersection of equity ownership and USCIS governance rules. Why? Well, majority ownership typically gives founders total operational control. But if you intend to use your own entity to sponsor your U.S. visa, unchecked majority ownership can actually work against you.   USCIS mandates require proof of an explicit and documented “employer-employee relationship,” meaning someone besides yourself must have clear “right of control” and operational authority over you. Most often, this independent authority is a board of directors, which must have the right to hire, evaluate, supervise and fire you. Simply put: For visa purposes, you cannot be your own boss.   International entrepreneurs seeking to self-sponsor walk a fine line; they need to demonstrate a legally compliant employer-employee relationship but don’t want to risk losing control of their equity stake or strategic vision.   That means baking proper corporate governance into the entity structure in three key areas:   Sitting as the sole board member while also serving as CEO isn’t going to fly in a self-sponsored visa application. Appointing your spouse, sibling or in-law to the board also won’t survive USCIS scrutiny.  Instead, bring on investors, experienced industry executives, venture advisors or respected professional peers. Then, grant your board real, documented authority to review your performance, set executive compensation and terminate employment.  Understandably, founders might fear that giving an independent board firing authority could put their role, and even their entire business, at risk. However, a corporate attorney can help you structure corporate architecture to separate your executive role from your shareholder rights. This can be accomplished through mechanisms such as dual-class stock, voting agreements and protective provisions that allow you to maintain long-term equity control and major shareholder voting power while still granting the independent board contractual oversight of your day-to-day employment as CEO.   A common mistake made by early-stage founders looking to self-sponsor is setting up an independent board on paper but leaving corporate bylaws unchanged. If your bylaws allow you as a majority shareholder to fire board members at will, the board’s authority isn’t real.  Your bylaws, board charters and executive employment agreement must explicitly delegate executive oversight and firing authority to the board. A corporate attorney can help you carve out protections that will protect your voting rights and equity, while still granting the board the necessary operational authority to satisfy immigration rules.  Additionally, many early-stage entrepreneurs rely on online templates to incorporate. While these tools are convenient and inexpensive, their default bylaws typically grant a majority shareholder absolute authority to appoint or remove board members. In USCIS’s view, this renders the board’s oversight authority meaningless. It’s worth it to spend just a few hours working with a corporate attorney to customize your bylaws to require specific notice periods, cause-based removal conditions or independent committee approvals for executive termination, all of which are essential to proving a genuine employer-employee relationship.   Restructuring your board or altering your bylaws shortly before filing a visa application can raise red flags. It’s important to establish your governance framework at initial formation and maintain a clear, documented history of oversight, including evidence that an independent board was formed, held meetings and maintained meeting minutes long before applying for a visa.  Strong corporate governance not only satisfies visa requirements; it also supports investor readiness. On Monday, a cyberattack affected refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets. Fréret spoke to Business Insider on Wednesday. The following has been translated from French and edited for length and clarity. Monday began like any other day at our supermarket. But at 5 a.m., our baker arrived and called us and said: "I think you need to come. There’s a big, big, big problem with the refrigeration." When we arrived, temperatures in all the refrigerated cabinets were rising. No circuit breaker had tripped, and the CO2 system was still running — but the control panel showed error after error. We put a thermometer in a freezer. It read 122 degrees Fahrenheit. That was when panic set in. We thought: This can’t be possible. We searched everywhere, restarted the refrigeration, and called the on-call technician. We were nowhere near imagining that someone had used the software to set temperatures above 122 degrees Fahrenheit. At about 7 a.m., we received an email from Danfoss, the company whose software monitors our refrigeration system, saying there had been a cyberattack. The whole system had failed, leaving nowhere to save the food. Everything that needs to stay cold was affected: fresh counters, frozen food, all of it. Staff were arriving to stock the shelves. We told them: "Stop, stop, stop, stop. We’re stopping the shelving." The temperatures kept rising. In some sections, they reached 122 degrees Fahrenheit. In the fish section, they climbed to about 163, even 176 degrees Fahrenheit. We shut down the motors, but it was too late. Butter and ice cream had melted. We called in a judicial officer to document what happened and take inventory before disposing of the food. We threw away about 30 cubic meters of food — a skip and a half — worth about $112,000, excluding equipment damage. Refrigeration systems are meant to make cold, not heat. At those temperatures, the fans melted. It was heartbreaking. We were sickened. Throwing away food is already such a concern in society. Having to put $112,000 worth in the bin was horrible. We’re a small rural community, so you ask yourself: Why us? We closed the fresh-food sections but kept the rest of the supermarket open. Some customers understood and asked how someone could do this. Others could not understand what a cyberattack had to do with food. They asked: "Why are you throwing away so much food? Why don’t you give it away?" But food that had reached 122 degrees Fahrenheit could not be given away. I had never imagined this could happen. You hear about cyberattacks on hospitals or cars. But attacking food? This was the first time I had ever seen anything like it. The software monitors food safety, alerting us when temperatures rise or a motor fails. From what we understand, someone changed the defrost settings. That system uses heat to stop refrigerators icing over; it had been set to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. We tried to save the food, but it heated up too fast. It was already too late. Still, I’m grateful for how the team responded. Morning staff came back that afternoon to clean the refrigerators. Nobody said, "That’s their problem." Everyone pulled together. We have disconnected the software from the internet. It still monitors temperatures of our refrigerators and freezers locally, but we can no longer check them remotely; we have to be at the store. We have not had another problem, but we are dealing with computers, so I can’t say it will never happen again. This episode has shown how vulnerable we are to cyberattacks. Demir is part of a global effort to collect data on how humans interact with the physical world, with the goal of building machines that can staff factories, clean homes, and even fight wars. Elon Musk, who is betting Tesla's future on the humanoid robot Optimus, has promoted a utopian future of "sustainable abundance," in which AI and robots make human labor largely optional. For now, those ambitions face a problem: a massive shortage of training data. "It is widely agreed in the robotics world that data is the key bottleneck," said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution who studies technology and industrial policy. This is the third installment of the AI Data Grab, Business Insider's series on how human work is becoming raw material for AI — and the companies that are cashing in. So far, we've reported on how AI labs are buying up employees' emails and Slack messages, and how law firms are turning decades of human expertise into AI systems. Now, the scramble is moving into the physical world, where companies are paying people to record skills robots have yet to learn. Contract workers in Mexico and the Philippines remotely control robots in American warehouses as they pack beauty products, recording movements so the machines can eventually do the work on their own. Other workers across the world strap cameras to their foreheads to capture first-person footage of themselves folding laundry and making hotel beds. "This is how the great knowledge transfer happens from humans to robots," said Josh Gruenstein, CEO of Tutor Intelligence. His company operates a Massachusetts "data factory" where workers remotely control robots to generate training data. Demand for robot training data is roughly 10 times higher than a year ago, Vineeth Velmurugan, who leads robot learning at the AI data startup Encord, said. Encord's customers, including Dyna Robotics and Agility Robotics, once requested 1,000 hours of annotated data. Now they want 10,000 or even 100,000, he said. That red-hot demand for real-world data comes as robotics has become one of Silicon Valley's hottest bets. Humanoid robot makers Figure AI and Agility Robotics have fetched multibillion-dollar valuations, as have the companies developing robot "brains" such as Skild AI and Physical Intelligence. Robotics companies raised $33.4 billion globally in the first half of this year, according to PitchBook data, surpassing the $28.7 billion raised in all of 2025. Cheaper hardware and computing, better AI models, labor shortages, and competition with China are all fueling investor interest. But a gulf remains between robots that perform impressive demos and machines reliable enough to work an eight-hour factory shift. Robotics companies hope more training data will help, and suppliers across the world, from scrappy startups to established companies like Scale AI, Instawork, and Uber, are rushing to sell it to them. Custom hardware is key to recording the physical world. Mecka AI, which has raised more than $120 million from investors including Sequoia and Nvidia, started with an app that paid people to record everyday activities two years ago. But the company soon ran into the limits of ordinary video. Mecka now designs headgear and sensor-equipped gloves to "sensorize humans," CEO Josh Gao said. The equipment records movements and force, such as the pressure needed to grip a glass or crack an egg. Contractors label workplace footage before Mecka sells it to AI labs and robotics companies. Microagi, the parent company of Shift, is expanding its collection efforts into homes and workplaces across more than 15 countries. It pays more than 35,000 people to record themselves performing physical tasks, CEO Bercan Kilic said. Shift said participants can earn up to $30 an hour and that it has paid out around $10 million in 2026. Household chores are the most common, but unusual tasks help expose models to unfamiliar situations. One contributor in Turkey records himself repairing old jet engines in his garage, Kilic said. Kilic's goal is to gather enough data to build robots that can work in factories and address labor shortages in Europe and the US. "If you run factories, the math is already on your desk," Kilic previously told Business Insider. "Your most experienced people retire this decade, and their replacements were never born. Reshoring only works if the robots do." For the workers supplying that data, though, the trade-off is income today in exchange for helping build machines that could eventually automate their work. Demir, the private chef, said he believes his work is safe. "Machines can just watch, listen, and follow instructions," he said. "They cannot feel or smell." The economics are different in countries where labor is cheaper. Human Archive, a data collection company based in San Francisco, began building operations in India last year through partnerships with gig platforms, hotels, and plumbing and electrical businesses. It started with an app that let people record audio and first-person video. The startup now also makes custom hardware in China, including camera-equipped headsets and wrist trackers that capture movement. Today, it operates in more than 30 countries and pays workers between $1 to $10 and "even much more," per hour, depending on how disruptive the equipment is, CEO Raj Patel said. These workers, Patel said, could earn "almost as much, or more [than their regular jobs], to just wear these devices." Mecka and Human Archive did not say how they ensure workers' consent when collecting data through partner businesses or local contractors. Shift said participation is voluntary, and some employees at partner businesses choose not to participate. The company said it obtains explicit consent, explaining what data is collected and how it is used, including that it may be licensed to other labs for AI and robotics training. The global competition for data work can come with a downside. It drives down wages and leaves workers with little bargaining power, said Mark Graham, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute and author of Feeding the Machine, a book about the labor behind AI. "Often the workers don't even know what they're doing," he said. "They're a very disposable appendage of a much bigger machine." The work can also be physically taxing. One operator who remotely controls robots in US warehouses from a Texas facility previously told Business Insider that eight-hour shifts cause arm and shoulder cramps. "We even have a massage gun in the office," they said. The companies collecting all this data are betting that the quest to train intelligent robots will fuel demand for years to come. Research firm Mordor Intelligence projects that the broader AI training dataset market will grow from $11.9 billion this year to nearly $49.8 billion by 2031. For robotics data suppliers, the bull case is that startups will spend a significant share of their funding on training material, said Siddharth Ramakrishnan, a partner at Scale Venture Partners. "If scaling laws continue to work, the pie will just keep growing," he said. But nobody knows how much data robots will need to work reliably, he added. If they need less than expected, data suppliers could lose business. If they need much more, investors could tire of paying before the robots become commercially viable. Some are betting that demand for robot training data is nowhere near its peak. Encord's Velmurugan likens today's robot brain to that of a two-year-old, and estimates that training a robot to work in homes — one of the hardest environments because it is so unstructured — could require a dataset five times the size of YouTube. At the end of 2025, YouTube held an estimated 29 billion videos, the equivalent of 280,000 years of footage, according to research firm Omdia. "It's hard to say how this will play out," Ken Goldberg, a UC Berkeley robotics professor and cofounder of warehouse robotics startup Ambi Robotics, said. "It might take five years or 50 years. And even if we had unlimited data now, I don't know if this approach will work," he said. Training robots in virtual environments, known as simulation, could also change the equation. World Labs, a startup slated for an $8.2 billion acquisition by AMD, says it can turn a small set of recordings into simulated environments and modify them to generate more training data for robots. If the technology delivers, robotics companies could need far less data from the physical world. But even sustained demand doesn't guarantee a profitable business. Earlier this year, Sam Padilla shut down his robotics data startup, Eidon AI, after struggling with logistics, upfront costs, and thin margins. He compared the business to dropshipping, where retailers sell goods shipped directly by suppliers and pocket the markup — until competitors offering the same products for less squeeze their margins. "There is a clear arbitrage opportunity to make money if you're willing to race and race to the bottom," he said. "But a technical bottleneck does not necessarily imply a good business."Have a tip? The culprit, as even occasional 9to5Mac readers are likely well aware by now, is the ongoing memory shortage, which has sent component costs soaring and squeezed device manufacturers, particularly those competing in lower-end markets. Apple came in second with 57.3 million shipped units, followed by Xiaomi, OPPO, and vivo. The report shows OPPO seeing the biggest drop among the top five, with shipments down 34.5% year over year, and Apple recording the smallest decline at 4%. This left Apple just 500,000 units behind Samsung, with a gap of only 0.2 percentage points in shipment share. Copied to clipboard Kevin Morse is on a mission to prove that a food business can be profitable while “adding value rather than extracting it.” As CEO and co-founder of Cairnspring Mills, he’s building modern mills in farming communities, buying identity-preserved grain from farmers and stone-milling it into exceptional flour. After more than a decade in the Skagit Valley, he’s opening Blue Mountain Mill in Pendleton, Oregon, with the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation. Below, he shares why wheat is a lot like wine, how his perfect site was the last place he looked and why slow, expensive dreams demand grit. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. What makes your product different?Wheat can be a lot more like wine grapes than most people realize and certainly not what I expected when I started diving into this business. I thought that wheat and flour were all the same. What I discovered totally surprised me. Most bakers have never had access to the diversity that actually exists in wheat. We’re trying to change that. We work with farmers to grow specific varieties, preserve their identity from the farm through the mill, and bring grains to market that previously weren’t available to most professional or home bakers. We also stone-mill our flour to preserve more of the natural flavor and nutrition of the grain. Of course, it still has to perform. A professional baker has to be able to depend on our flour every day. So the challenge—and the fun—is delivering flavor, nutrition and identity while producing flour that performs exceptionally well. What is different about the business structure?We’re organized as a social-purpose corporation, which gives us the fiduciary flexibility to consider outcomes beyond simply maximizing profit. That can sound abstract, but for us it translates into very practical decisions. We can donate flour to food banks because feeding people in our community matters. We can give an incremental price break to a young bakery that’s just getting started because helping them succeed may create a great customer and community business for the next 20 years. We can pay a farmer more for growing something differently because we believe there is long-term value in healthier soil. Those decisions may not maximize the profit on that particular transaction, but they can create enormous value over time. That’s an important distinction for me. We aren’t trying to give value away; we’re trying to keep adding value rather than extracting it. Our investors are part of that. Their capital makes this work possible, and we have a responsibility to build a business that earns them a return. We still have to build a financially strong, profitable company. Profit gives us the ability to keep investing in farmers, employees, customers, and communities while rewarding the people who invested in us. It just isn’t the only outcome we measure. Can you summarize farmers’ plight and how you’re aiming to help?Commodity agriculture has become a race to the bottom. Farmers carry tremendous risk—weather, markets, equipment, land and rising input costs—but in most cases they have very little control over the price they’re paid. The pressure is constant to get bigger, produce more and lower costs. We’re trying, in our small way, to create an alternative. Rather than asking how cheaply we can buy wheat, we’re trying to create a higher-value domestic market for farmers. We contract directly with growers, create markets for differentiated varieties and regenerative practices, and provide greater predictability around what we’re going to buy and what we’re going to pay. If we do it well, farmers get a better, more predictable bottom line, while also having more opportunity to invest in the long-term health and viability of their soil and farm. I keep coming back to the idea that regenerative agriculture also has to be economically regenerative. We can’t ask farmers to improve the health of the land while participating in an economic system that slowly puts them out of business. What made you decide that this was the right time to open Blue Mountain Mill in Pendleton, Oregon?Blue Mountain is the result of more than a decade of learning at our first mill in the Skagit Valley. We demonstrated demand for what we were doing and eventually reached the point where our ambitions and customer demand outgrew what that mill could produce. Pendleton also has three things that are incredibly important to our model: access to some of the best wheat-growing land in the country, access to the markets we want to serve, and an existing community of farmers already practicing regenerative agriculture. That combination is difficult to find. We also knew a second mill would allow us to test whether the model we’ve developed in Skagit could work at a significantly larger scale and in another region. There was no moment when all the risk disappeared and it suddenly became obvious that we should build it. At some point, as an entrepreneur, you have to decide whether you’ve learned enough, whether the opportunity is real, and whether you’re willing to take the next risk. We decided we were. How did you arrive at the partnership with the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation?Ironically, the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation location was the last place I looked. We originally wanted fee-simple property that we could purchase outright. I probably looked at 20 different sites, and for one reason or another, none of them felt right. I had been encouraged to look at Coyote Business Park on the Umatilla Indian Reservation, but because it didn’t fit that original model, I kept looking elsewhere. Eventually, I agreed to go see it. The infrastructure and access were nearly perfect for what we needed—and it didn’t hurt that the site has an incredible view of the Blue Mountains. But what ultimately sealed the deal was something I hadn’t been looking for on a real estate checklist: alignment with the Tribe. As we got to know one another, we discovered shared values around stewardship, agriculture, community, economic development and building something that could create lasting value in the region. What began as a search for a piece of real estate became a much deeper partnership. There’s probably an entrepreneurial lesson in that for me. Sometimes being too constrained by what you think the answer is supposed to look like prevents you from seeing a much better answer sitting right in front of you. Milling infrastructure isn’t a software business — it’s slow, physical and expensive. What would you tell a founder who’s drawn to a similarly capital-heavy, long-payback idea about whether it’s worth it?If you’re looking to make a quick fortune, this probably isn’t the business for you. Building physical infrastructure requires an enormous amount of patience, commitment and perseverance. It will probably take longer than you think, cost more than you think, and present problems you couldn’t possibly have anticipated when you started. You need capital, obviously, but you also need grit. There have been plenty of times during Cairnspring’s journey when the easiest or most conventional answer would have been to stop. We kept looking for another path. That doesn’t mean blindly sticking with a bad idea. Caring about the mission doesn’t excuse you from making good business decisions. You have to be rigorous about costs, demand and how the business will earn a return on the capital it takes to build it. You have to constantly listen, learn and adapt. But I’ve learned there’s an important difference between being flexible about how you get somewhere and being committed to where you’re trying to go. What’s something about running a social-purpose corporation that surprised you — harder or easier than you expected?One thing I’ve learned is that having a social purpose doesn’t necessarily make decisions easier. Sometimes it makes them harder because you’re intentionally considering more than one outcome. It’s relatively easy to maximize a single variable. It gets more complicated when you’re asking what’s best for the financial health of the company, our employees, farmers, customers, communities and the environment—and those answers don’t always point in exactly the same direction. The surprising part is that I’ve also seen how often those interests reinforce each other over the long term. Helping a young bakery get established can create a loyal customer. Paying a farmer fairly can create a dependable long-term supply relationship. Investing in employees creates people who are deeply committed to the company. I’ve become less interested in whether something maximizes the value of an individual transaction and more interested in whether we’re creating lasting value through the relationship. That doesn’t remove the tension. We still have to make money, and sometimes we have to make difficult decisions. But the social-purpose structure gives us permission to define success more broadly than the next quarter’s bottom line. Photo credit: Andrew M.
