I’d like Cairnspring to help demonstrate that regional, human-scale food infrastructure can be economically successful while creating value far beyond the bottom line. Our vision is a world nourished by cleaner, healthier grains grown regeneratively and milled close to home. Success would mean healthier soil, more nutritious and flavorful food, prosperous farmers, good jobs, thriving local businesses and communities that are more resilient because some of the infrastructure and economic value of their food system has returned home. I’d also like what we’re doing to inspire others. Cairnspring doesn’t need to own every mill, and we’re certainly not going to solve these problems ourselves. In fact, real success would mean other entrepreneurs, farmers and communities take what we’ve learned, improve upon it and build models of their own. TOPICS                      personal tech                           AI's appetite for components hammers budget handsets, with analysts seeing little relief before 2028      Smartphone shipments fell by at least a fifth in the third calendar quarter as the AI-driven memory crunch battered another consumer hardware market. Preliminary estimates from IDC and Omdia put the year-on-year decline at 22 percent and 20 percent respectively. Memory costs have surged by approximately 350 percent since last year, according to IDC, and are still rising. This continues to place substantial pressure on vendor margins, prompting them to hike price tags and scale back on devices at the value end of the market. IDC estimates that vendors shipped 255.3 million smartphones into distribution channels and warns that the downturn is far from over. "The sharp downturn the industry has been bracing for finally materialized in the third quarter this year. However, the worst is yet to come," said Nabila Popal, IDC's senior research director for worldwide devices. "Current indicators suggest that the market has not yet reached the bottom. While memory inflation is beginning to slow down, with a low double-digit sequential increase in Q3 compared to a 50 to 100 percent jump in prior quarters, costs remain elevated across other critical components as well, compounding the crunch." Omdia puts shipments at roughly 255 million, close to IDC's estimate despite the different annual decline. It says that the shrinking market has further polarized the competitive landscape, with Samsung and Apple now accounting for about 45 percent of global shipments, up approximately 8 percentage points from a year ago, while rising costs hit more price-sensitive segments particularly hard. Omdia still expects global smartphone shipments to fall 12 percent across 2026, followed by another 6 percent decline next year. It previously forecast that devices priced above $400 would prove more resilient and could record shipment growth. "We don't anticipate any relief to the current memory crisis before 2028 at the earliest as we expect there to remain a considerable gap between demand and supply. The first signs of improvement we're looking for is when the memory pricing will stabilize (basically stopping to grow), and we're still not there yet," Omdia principal analyst Runar Bjorhovde told The Register. Omdia says investment in distribution partnerships and premium devices could determine which vendors emerge stronger when costs ease. New flagship launches, promotions, and festive demand in Q4 are unlikely to fully offset persistent supply-side pressures. Omdia reckons buyers may get used to paying more, potentially creating greater opportunities for higher-value devices. The firm previously outlined the measures some phone makers are taking to offset the rising cost of memory parts, including switching to cheaper display panels, sensors, or radio frequency (RF) modules. IDC also sees little prospect of recovery before 2028 and expects a lasting shift toward higher costs. Google has started changing its search results and Google Play fees, the European Commission said, as it reviews compliance. Google’s offices in London The European Commission is in talks with Google about the steps the company may take following the EU’s €890M (about $1bn) fine in July. The Commission confirmed the talks on Wednesday to Reuters. The fines were issued under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), the EU law that sets rules for the largest online platforms. In its July decision, the Commission fined Google €460M for placing its own shopping, hotel, transport and sports results above rival services in search. It also fined the company €430m for stopping app developers from pointing users to cheaper offers outside Google Play, such as on their own websites or in other app stores. At the same time, the Commission ordered Google to treat rival services in search fairly and to let developers steer users away from its app store. They gave the company 60 days to comply, or face daily penalty payments of up to 5% of its average daily worldwide turnover. According to the Commission, Google has since started changing how it displays search results. Moreover, it has also announced, and in part introduced, changes to the fees it charges developers on Google Play. “We are currently in dialogue with Google, so I’ll not prejudge the outcome of this dialogue,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said, according to Reuters. The Commission added that it will carefully assess Google’s measures. As part of that review, it will also seek views from companies in the market and other third parties. Google criticised the decision when it was announced. Kent Walker, Google’s president of global affairs, said the ruling would force it to remove real-time search features, such as live hotel and flight prices. “This isn’t fair competition,” Walker said at the time. The July fine was the first DMA penalty against Google. However, it is not the company’s only case under the law. Earlier this year, Google also offered the Commission changes to its news-search ranking to settle a separate DMA investigation. Edited by Corinne Reichert  October 15, 2026, 6:14 pm ET Trying to remember things yourself is so yesterday — or so AI-wearable makers want you to believe. Amazon on Thursday announced two new products, the Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse, which use AI to record conversations and then process them into “summaries, to-dos, reminders and insights.” The Frontier can be worn on your wrist or your clothes, and the Eclipse attaches magnetically to the back of your phone. They are both from Amazon Bee, which is the company’s lineup of AI-powered personal assistant devices and software. Amazon acquired AI-wearable company Bee in July 2025. There are several ways you might use the devices. Maybe you’re talking with a friend at the coffee shop about details you’ll want to remember later. The Bee Frontier — on your wrist or clipped to your clothes — can record the conversation and give you a transcript or summary, much like AI tools like Gemini can do during a business meeting. The Bee Eclipse, attached to the back of your phone, can record your phone calls and give you transcripts and summaries of your calls. More from CNET Just make sure you ask your conversation partners if they mind being recorded. Amazon says you can also review memories to remember conversation details, and Bee can recommend personalized goals and actions, depending on themes or trends it picks up on. “The more you use Bee, the smarter it becomes, learning your unique patterns, preferences and relationships, building a progressively smarter understanding of your world without demanding attention,” an Amazon spokesperson told CNET via email. You can view all the output in the Bee mobile or desktop app. The Bee Frontier costs $75, and the Bee Eclipse will cost $100, though the Eclipse is not yet available. Users can pick between two tiers of service: The free one allows you to get conversation summaries and recaps for up to 14 days, while the Bee Pro subscription costs $12 per month, which gets you a personal chat assistant and provides unlimited memory, integrations with Amazon, Alexa Plus and third-party apps and suggests to-do lists. The Frontier can be worn on the wrist or attached to your clothes. It’s made out of ultrasoft silicone and comes in three colors — lavender, sage and onyx. A fully charged battery can last up to seven days and uses USB-C charging. The device has dual microphones and advanced noise filtering for crowded and loud places. Audio recording begins by pressing a button, and a light goes on to show that it’s recording. You can also configure it to stop if there has not been sound for a certain period. The size of a credit card, the Eclipse can magnetically attach to the back of a phone and comes in four colors — silver, midnight, honey and blush. A fully charged battery can last three weeks and maybe more, according to Amazon. You begin and stop recording with the Eclipse by pressing a button, and an LED light goes on to indicate that recording is in progress. Amazon said the Bee Frontier and Eclipse can connect to Alexa Plus, Amazon’s new AI-powered assistant, and also Amazon.com. So, instead of getting conversation summaries, insights and to-dos by looking at the Bee app on your phone, you could just ask Alexa Plus to read them to you. When connected to Amazon, the Bee device can present shopping recommendations on the Amazon home page or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps. For example, say your friend recommends a certain book while talking to you. The Frontier or Eclipse will hear that, locate it on Amazon and show that listing to you. You can also link the Frontier and Eclipse to other apps, such as Gmail, Microsoft Outlook and Google Calendar. Amazon said Bee devices can draft emails and create calendar invites based on recorded conversations. Bee devices can also connect to your Apple HealthKit “to build a more complete picture of your wellness,” Amazon said. Amazon said it does not store recorded audio, and you can neither access nor share it. You’ll be prompted to get permission from callers when those calls are being recorded, but it is not mandatory — the recording will still happen.  Expect the AI accessories market to grow. “Who doesn’t want to stop forgetting names and dinner plans?” asks Jon Rettinger, a tech tester with more than 1.66 million subscribers to his YouTube channel. But Rettinger said that invasion of privacy could be an issue, especially for people being recorded by someone using the Bee Frontier and Eclipse. There are 12 states in the US where it is legally required that callers be notified that they are being recorded, known as “all-party consent.” “The people around you never agreed to any of it, and a little light on your wrist isn’t much of a warning,” Rettinger told CNET. “In California, you legally need everyone’s consent to record a private conversation, and I’d guess most people buying these have no clue. For a work meeting where everybody knows it’s on, great. Wearing it all day is a different story.” Amazon says Bee Private Compute — a security system built into both devices — processes conversations inside a secure and isolated environment “where no one, including Amazon, can access your data.” After audio is recorded and processed into insights in real time, it is deleted, Amazon said. No one can get to your insights data unless you share it, and conversation transcripts are encrypted and are not accessible unless you choose to share them. You can delete transcripts and summaries whenever you want in the app.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

John Ternus sat down with TIME for a wide-ranging interview centered on iPhone Duo, but also covering a variety of other topics, including AI. Regarding the iPhone Duo, which is hitting the market nearly a decade after other foldables, Ternus was involved in early foldable work at Apple all the way back in 2011. In 2011, when many people still carried around flip phones, Ternus and five other engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, exploring what kind of batteries and circuit boards might be needed for such an idea. “It felt clear that we were going to eventually get to a place where OLED displays were going to be flexible,” Ternus says. Ternus wasn’t a fan of early attempts at foldables from other companies in the 2010s. He says, “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy.” The drive to achieve a foldable unlike its competitors is evidenced by a story from Richard Dinh, Apple’s VP of Product Design. Along the way, Ternus encouraged the team to invest more time and effort in the project, even as other foldables beat them to market. Dinh says that at one point, he asked Ternus whether his team should proceed with a top surface material similar to those of its competitors, which Dinh felt had flaws but was potentially good enough. “And he was like, ‘Look, Rich, you’ll know when it’s the right thing.’ And that gave us the confidence to really push the boundaries on innovation and manufacturing, and fly worldwide to connect our suppliers together and come up with the nanotexture [a surface technology],” Dinh says. The result—a surface made from a custom polymer and built atop a hinge with more than 100 tiny interior precision components—has impressed its first users, who have said they can barely detect a crease at all. Back in 2015, I was working for a SaaS company that I'd founded. It mostly served clients in the restaurant industry, where my parents and grandparents were both entrepreneurs. One day, I was meeting with an out-of-town client who was staying in Manhattan Beach. He mentioned he'd rented the BMW he was driving from Relay Ride (which later became the car rental app Turo). That was the first time I heard of car sharing. I was working from home, and my Smartcar was definitely an underutilized asset. On a whim, I listed it for rent. A grad student at UCLA booked it for three months, and I pretty much never saw that car again — after that, it was always rented. My day-to-day car use was pretty minimal, but I still needed to drive occasionally. I leased another Smartcar because they were very cheap at the time. I listed that one too, and soon acquired a third car. At the time, I was about 25. I couldn't afford to buy real estate to get into the short-term rental market. But renting cars gave me an accessible way to turn an underutilized asset into a productive asset. My friends and family thought I was crazy, but I loved the business's efficiency. I began researching what cars were most in demand in greater LA. I bought mid-range luxury cars like Corvettes and BMWs, which were popular with tourists. Before long, I had a fleet of more than 50 cars and was making hundreds of thousands annually. A little more than a year after I started renting, a client offered to buy my SaaS company. It wasn't a hugely profitable sale, but the timing was good because it allowed me to expand my rental business. I also started a YouTube channel teaching other entrepreneurs how to manage their fleets. That was hard to monetize, so rentals accounted for about 90% of my income. I learned a lot about operations and logistics. At first, I had cars parked all over my neighborhood in free public parking. Eventually, I leased a small lot. In my own businesses and in the work I do with clients, I’ve always tried to find ways to market effectively without spending a fortune. I actually enjoy the constraint. Having a limited budget forces you to think more creatively, experiment with ideas you might otherwise overlook and find ways to use the resources you already have. Over the years, some of those experiments have worked surprisingly well. They’ve taught me that good marketing doesn’t always require a big advertising budget — sometimes it just requires looking at your business from a different angle. Here are some of the low-cost strategies I’ve used myself and with my clients. I discovered the potential of auctions almost by accident. When I sold a few cars from my rental car business through an auction, I ended up getting a surprisingly good price. It made me realize that auctions can do more than help you sell something — they can create competition and attract attention at the same time. When several people want the same product, they’re no longer negotiating only with you; they’re competing with one another. According to Bidbus, auction prices were 4.51% higher with two bidders than with one and nearly 10% higher when five or more bidders participated. You don’t have to auction off your entire inventory to test the idea. Try one product, a service package or even a limited number of available spots. There are platforms where you can run an auction for a relatively small fee, making it an inexpensive experiment for the right type of business. And even though only the winning bidder makes the purchase, everyone who watches, shares or participates in the auction is interacting with your brand. That turns the auction itself into a marketing event, not just a way to make a sale. When I was a young entrepreneur, a friend and I ran a small bike shop. We would buy used bikes, fix them up and resell them. We didn’t have much of a marketing budget, so instead of trying to bring customers to us, we went to where they already were. We would load around 10 bikes into a van, drive to local sporting events and offer free test rides to anyone interested. That turned out to be even more valuable than simply putting the bikes in front of the right audience. People could actually ride them, see how they felt and experience the product before deciding whether to buy. According to TLG, 61% of consumers say they are more inclined to make a purchase after attending a live event. You can apply the same principle to almost any small business. Find out where your ideal customers already spend their time, then look for an inexpensive way to let them experience what you sell through samples, demonstrations, trials or small events. Instead of spending your limited marketing budget trying to bring a broad audience to you, go to the right audience and give them a reason to try your product. According to ZenMux, 48% of small businesses are already using AI in their marketing, including for writing email and social media copy, creating visual content and analyzing data. But using AI doesn’t necessarily mean using it efficiently. It’s easy to default to the most powerful — and often most expensive — model for every task, even when much of your everyday marketing work doesn’t require it. In my businesses, I try to match the model to the job. I use cheaper, faster models for high-volume tasks such as brainstorming headlines, creating variations of social posts or rewriting product descriptions, and reserve premium models for work that requires deeper reasoning, research or more nuanced writing. There’s little reason to pay for the most capable model when a less expensive one can produce the result you need. The difference might amount to very little on a single prompt, but it becomes meaningful when AI is embedded into your everyday marketing workflow. Across hundreds or thousands of tasks, those small costs add up. Instead of automatically using the best model available, use the most cost-effective model that can reliably do the job. I always pay people who refer clients to my businesses — even when they tell me not to. If someone sends me a client, I’ll get their PayPal or bank details and send them a referral fee. If that client continues working with us, I keep paying the referral every month. Sometimes people tell me, “You really don’t need to send me anything.” My answer is simple: It’s my rule. You can donate the money to charity or spend it however you like, but I’m still going to pay you. And if someone refuses the money altogether or sends it back, I’ll offer them one of my services for free instead. I want people who help my business grow to get something in return. There’s a business reason behind that rule. Referrals can be one of the lowest-cost ways to acquire customers because you’re not starting from zero — the person recommending you has already transferred some of their trust to your business. According to Tailor Brands, 92% of people trust referrals from people they know. That’s why I don’t treat referrals as a lucky bonus or simply hope that satisfied customers will spread the word. I reward them deliberately and make referrals part of how I market my businesses. When I take on a small business as a client, one of the processes I use is a questionnaire that helps identify opportunities to turn the work they’re already doing into visual content. The idea is simple: Don’t create something just for marketing — document the customer experience that already exists. A restaurant can capture dishes being prepared and served, a gardening company can show a yard before, during and after a job, and a home improvement business can document an entire renovation from the first day to the finished result. There’s a good reason to make this content visual. According to research, 60% of consumers always look for photos or videos before purchasing a product. Social media also gives small businesses an inexpensive way to put that content in front of potential customers. Seventy-six percent of small and midsize businesses say social media has had a positive impact on their business performance. I’ve found this works particularly well for small businesses because it can be incredibly cheap to execute. Ask employees to take photos and short videos while they work, do it yourself, hire a photographer for just a few hours to build a library of professional material, or give satisfied customers a small incentive to share photos and videos of their experience. Once you have the content, distribution can cost virtually nothing. Build visual libraries on Instagram and Pinterest, add galleries to your website, and upload videos to YouTube or Vimeo.  During the slower winter months, my rental car business sometimes has cars sitting unused for days. Rather than leave them parked, we’ve offered them free for a few days to travel vloggers and other creators visiting our city. It helps them explore the area and create better content about the destination, while we ask for something relatively small in return: a mention of our business, sometimes just a 20- or 30-second segment in a video they were already planning to publish. I particularly like this approach when there’s a natural connection between what you give away and the audience you want to reach. A travel creator visiting your city already has an audience interested in travel, so a local car rental recommendation makes sense within their content. According to Adam Collins, three in four consumers say they’re more likely to spend money at a local business if it supports community issues or charitable causes. Look for similar opportunities to support local creators, events and organizations with something your business can provide inexpensively. The key is to think beyond cash when deciding what you can spend on marketing. A restaurant might provide food for a local event, a gym could offer its space to a community group, and a service business could donate its expertise. Something that costs your business very little to provide can be genuinely useful to someone else while introducing your brand to a relevant new audience. Some of your best marketing ideas may already be sitting in your inbox. We recently took on a client and went through the questions their customers were already asking in emails, phone calls, sales conversations and support requests. We then turned those recurring questions into useful content that answered them directly. It didn’t require expensive topic research or a complicated content strategy, yet after implementing the approach, the client’s visibility in AI-generated answers increased by almost 400%. There’s a broader reason this works. According to Discovered Labs, its analysis of 2 million AI citations found that pages that more closely matched what users were asking received significantly more citations — about 30% more for a meaningful increase in alignment. In other words, the questions your customers ask you every day can also be clues to what potential customers are asking search engines and AI tools. Start keeping track of those questions and turn the recurring ones into blog posts, guides and FAQ pages. You’re essentially turning conversations your business is already having into inexpensive marketing assets that can keep attracting potential customers long after you publish them. Cold outreach can be one of the most affordable ways for a small business to start conversations with potential customers, especially when AI sales agents can automate much of the repetitive work, from prospecting and research to sending emails and following up. The key is to use automation where it saves time without automating the entire relationship. According to Instantly, 58% of replies come from the first email, while the remaining 42% come from follow-ups. That’s why I always build two or three automated follow-ups into my outreach campaigns rather than relying on a single message. But the moment someone replies, I go old-school. I take over the conversation personally and leave AI agents and automated responses out of it. When inboxes are increasingly filled with AI-generated outreach, a genuine human conversation can be one of the simplest ways to stand out. The goal isn’t to automate sales from beginning to end; it’s to use AI to do the repetitive work cheaply and consistently, then spend your time where the human element matters most. There is science behind why we sometimes feel a little good when folks around us feel a little bad. It's a part of human nature, and we shouldn't judge ourselves too hard for feeling it. It's good to indulge every now and again, just to make sure that we're still human. That's what we're here to do today with these design fails.  It's natural to want to see things go a little poorly every now and again. It makes us feel like we're doing okay. I know I need a little reassurance every now and again that I'm doing the right thing and that I'm in the right place. Who feels like they've got all that stuff nailed down all of the time? I'm often in need of a little boost. A little reminder that I'm actually doing fine and some of my worries are a little bit unfounded. There is nothing wrong with zooming out sometimes and taking stock of not only the things that go wrong, but the things that go right. And sometimes stealing a little bit of joy from someone else is just what the doctor ordered. Maybe you need to see your enemy fail a little bit. I know it's not the healthiest impulse, but it's an impulse nonetheless, and it's all going to be okay. It's why we keep coming back to Fail Blog. We've been doing this for quite some time, and we have no intention of slowing down.  Have you ever seen a sign on the side of the road or in a restaurant or in a newspaper that had a typo or a misuse of a word and you immediately felt a little pep in your step? That's natural. We like to feel smart and like we have the ability to point out things that others might miss. This list is all about celebrating those moments. Those fails. That thing that went off the rails that now we can all laugh at together. Life is hard, no matter who you are or where you're coming from. It's important to stop and smell the roses when you can. Or you can just smile at the misfortune of someone else and feel a little smug about it. There is no rule against that. In fact, it is encouraged here, and we would never stop you from wanting to feel that. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kenny Totten, a 38-year-old founder based in Orlando. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I've been a Delta SkyMiles member for the last 14 years, and I've had Delta's Diamond Medallion status — their highest loyalty tier — for the past seven years. As a Delta loyalist, there was nothing sadder than the news that they passed up Starlink. I'm the cofounder of AllFly, a travel startup, and I travel for work about 15 to 20 times a year. Being connected on the plane is the No. 1 priority for me. After flying a United flight in July that included Starlink, it was enough reason for me to switch. In July, I had to go home to New Jersey for a funeral. I booked a last-minute flight from Orlando to Newark on United, as I was looking for a direct flight. Given the circumstances, I wasn't looking for Starlink. Having worked in travel, I knew people were clamoring about Starlink, but I hadn't gotten to experience it yet. I didn't see any notifications before my flight about it being a Starlink flight. That day, I sat down in my seat, and my seatback screen notified me that the plane had Starlink. It was a pleasant surprise. I took the opportunity to connect on my laptop immediately. It was nice that from the moment you entered the plane, you could be on the internet, rather than waiting until you were in the air or above a certain altitude. I needed to edit a video on CapCut for an upcoming social media campaign. I used Starlink to download a video, and then upload it and send it to a teammate for them to work on, too. I was also able to send pictures. We were building an internal app, and so I vibe-coded fully on Replit using Starlink. I had a lot of tabs open and had Claude running. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    It was amazing, like being on the internet at my house, in my living room— that's how fast it is. For the two-hour flight, I was just doing work. As a founder, I don't get the luxury of being able to log off for a few hours in the middle of the day. When Slack and email are going, or I'm collaborating and working with teammates, or I'm building an app, I want to have fast internet. If I'm going to be on the plane for two or three hours, it's so beneficial to be able to get things done in the air and work as if I'm at home, instead of losing a few hours. For leisure, or if I travel on the weekends, Starlink is a little less essential. I seldom log on and work on weekend flights. I'm a big TV and movie guy, and I can just download movies or shows to my iPad and brain-rot. I was so hopeful that my flight would have Starlink too. It didn't. It was such a letdown because I'd just experienced something so magical, and then I had to go back to the normal United Wi-Fi. (Editor's note: In a July 2026 press release, United said it expects that nearly 1,000 aircraft will be Starlink-equipped by the end of the year.) I tried logging into Replit so I could continue vibe coding. It couldn't even hold a connection — it was horrible. I gave up and just listened to a podcast. In my experience, normal Delta WiFi is much better than normal United WiFi. On Delta, you're able to browse the internet, be on Slack or Microsoft Teams, and do light work. You could watch videos, but sometimes the buffering is a little slow. It really struggles with downloading and uploading; sending a photo or a document on Delta WiFi would rarely go through for me. On most Delta flights that I'm on, there's at least some segment of the flight during which the internet goes out for a period of time, whether for a few minutes or 20 minutes. The reliability of the uptime leaves a bit to be desired. Connecting and using anything intensive is a pain. I don't think I've been able to do anything more than being on Replit or doing some work with Claude or ChatGPT. I'd go out of my way to maintain my Delta status; if there was a direct United flight and a Delta flight with a connection, I would take the Delta flight. In the past, I'd book Delta even if it cost up to around $100 more. It's so hard to get status on airlines — you have to spend a lot of money and travel extensively — so I jumped at United's offer to match my status to Premier 1K for 120 days. I applied and had my status matched within two days. United has to compete, and status matching is how you win travelers from the other guy. If Delta suddenly handed out Diamond status to a bunch of people, and clubs were more crowded and upgrades got harder, I'd be ticked off too, but I get the business side. If United does a good job with its Starlink rollout, I could see myself splitting my time between Delta and United. For United, in order to maintain my status for the following year, I have to either fly 20 qualifying flights or earn 7,500 qualifying points (equal to spending $7,500 on flights) within 120 days, which would be extremely hard for me, so my 1K status may be short-lived. I get my Delta status through spending on my Delta Business Reserve credit card, so my Delta status will likely never be in jeopardy. When I can fly somewhere directly on United and prices are comparable, I think United will win for me in the future. Price, schedule, and times are all factors, but if everything else is close, I'd pick a Starlink flight if I'm flying more than two hours, especially during the workweek. The problem is, at the current moment, I can't easily tell which flights have it. Delta still wins when it's the direct flight option, better price, or better schedule. I would rather fly Delta everywhere, but now its free WiFi is inferior. Nearly all of Delta's peers went with StarLink, while Delta went with Amazon Leo, which won't be out until 2028. I hope Delta takes stock of all the online chatter and listens to its customers. It has done a great job in the past of continually improving its product and listening to its customers. It was one of the first airlines in America to offer free WiFi, which has always been a staple, so the whole Starlink dustup is surprising. For the most profitable and what I feel is the most premium airline in America, it seems odd for Delta not to outfit its planes with the best in-flight internet. A Delta spokesperson said, "We're grateful for the loyalty of our customers and remain focused on earning it every time they fly with us. Delta continues to invest in strengthening our connected network and we're proud to offer an award-winning, premium travel experience with elevated products, loyalty benefits and the signature hospitality that Delta is known for." The government hopes a weaker dinar will help pay salaries, but traders face rising import costs and uncertainty. Save Share Baghdad, Iraq – Sitting anxiously in his small office in Jameela market, one of Baghdad’s main wholesale markets, food trader Hamza al-Rudayni is waiting to see what the coming days will bring. A decision by the Iraqi government to devalue the country’s currency, the dinar, against the US dollar has left traders like him facing sudden losses and uncertainty over the prices they should charge for their goods. “I don’t know what to do,” al-Rudayni told Al Jazeera after the devaluation reduced the dollar value of his dinar holdings, leaving him with less money to purchase imported goods. “All I know is I woke up a few days ago to discover that I had lost 25 million Iraqi dinars (roughly $16,500 at the new exchange rate) because of this decision, while larger merchants lost billions,” he said. Al-Rudayni entered the wholesale trade market last year after losing his previous job at a private Iraqi bank that he says was sanctioned by the United States Treasury. He sold his car and used his savings to start trading with a larger merchant before recently launching his own business. With exchange-rate fluctuations making prices unpredictable, al-Rudayni said he and many other traders have chosen to suspend buying and selling until the situation stabilises. “Market activity has ground to a halt,” al-Rudayni said. “Traders buy goods in dollars but sell them in dinars, as regulations prohibit them from selling in dollars.” That is the root of the problem for traders: A weaker dinar means they have to pay more in local currency for goods imported in dollars, while making it harder to determine the right price they should charge customers for goods they already have in stock. On October 7, the Iraqi government introduced a new official exchange rate against the US dollar, in an attempt to ease a financial crisis triggered by the US-Israeli war on Iran and the  disruption of oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz. Before the war, Iraq exported around 3.5 million barrels of oil per day through the Strait of Hormuz, accounting for 90 percent of Iraq’s government revenue. The Central Bank of Iraq decision set the rate at 1,520 dinars per US dollar for cash sales to the public. It was previously set at 1,320 dinars per dollar. Devaluing the Iraqi dinar by almost 15 percent against the dollar allows the government to receive more local currency for every dollar of oil revenue it converts, helping it cover public spending, including government employee salaries. “It is my decision and I am responsible for it,” Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said during a meeting with parliamentary leaders on Thursday. “I was facing three challenging options to cover salaries and other mandatory expenditures,” al-Zaidi added. “The first is to cut salaries by 35 percent … the second is to pay the salaries every 45 days … while the third is to resort to foreign loans.” Al-Zaidi, a former banker, also said that his government had inherited public debt exceeding 208 trillion Iraqi dinars ($139bn at the new rate) when it took office in May. He said the government needed approximately 10 trillion dinars ($6.7bn) each month to cover salaries and other essential expenditure.      The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz had caused a severe financial squeeze for the Iraqi government. Although the situation has eased somewhat in recent weeks after Iraq’s oil exports partially recovered, they have yet to return to their pre-war levels. Mudher Mohammed Salih, the Iraqi prime minister’s financial adviser, said in August that the Central Bank of Iraq’s foreign currency reserves had declined from $106bn to approximately $80bn. To make up for the loss of revenue, the Iraqi government has also turned to borrowing from domestic banks to cover salaries and other expenses. A Finance Ministry official told Al Jazeera that ensuring salaries were paid on time remained the government’s main priority, describing this issue as a matter of domestic economic stability. “Our hands are tied regarding the revenue and how to maintain enough money to ensure that we can pay the salaries,” the official, who asked to remain anonymous because he was not authorised to speak publicly, said. Economists have warned that while adjusting the exchange rate could ease some immediate fiscal pressures, it would not address the deeper weaknesses in Iraq’s economy. “Nothing in economics is sacred, including the exchange rate,” said Nabil al-Marsoumi, professor of economics at Al Maaqal University in Basra. “It can be adjusted, but only after all other options have been exhausted.” “In any case, the exchange rate shouldn’t be used as a cover-up for failures in the state’s economic and fiscal policies,” he added. Universal Cart is rolling out in the U.S. across Search and the Gemini app, with checkout inside the cart or a one-way handoff to the store's own site. Google is launching Universal Cart in the United States through both Google Search and its Gemini app. The Universal Cart allows customers to add items from multiple different retailers into it, also provides price drop notifications and stock replenishment notices; allows users to complete checkout using either Google Pay or simply go to the retailer’s website at participating stores. In a blog post announcing the launch Suresh Ganapathy stated that he was Senior Director of Product Management for Consumer Shopping. Google had initially announced the Universal Cart during I/O in May. You can add products from several stores while shopping in Search, including AI Mode, or in the Gemini app, and keep everything together in one cart across both. You’ll also get alerts when a saved item drops in price or comes back in stock. It’s built on Google Wallet, so it can suggest which of a shopper’s cards to use based on each card’s perks. It also shows promo codes in the cart. Merchants Google names for in-cart checkout or cart transfer include Nike, Sephora, Target, Ulta Beauty, Walmart, Wayfair, and many Shopify merchants. The merchant stays the seller of record either way. In its I/O post (which we covered at the time), Google stated that it expected Search and the Gemini app in the United States to have access to the shopping cart by the end of Summer. The same post stated that YouTube and Gmail would get this functionality later. The new post does not contain any information regarding YouTube and Gmail. Additionally, the original May post included historical pricing for items, warnings that products in your Shopping Cart will not function together, as well as loyalty program information related to Google Wallet. None of these features are mentioned within today’s post. It is possible they were included; however, the Launch Post does not include descriptions of these capabilities. In May, Google described Universal Cart as “the next step that brings this all together” for the agentic commerce foundation it had been building. Today’s post separates agentic features that act on a shopper’s behalf from tools that “give shoppers confidence and control,” and places the cart in the second group. Google’s developer docs tie the cart’s transfer option to the Cart API in the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP). The Cart API guide says the API supports Universal Cart by creating a cart on the merchant’s system, through a CreateCart call, when a shopper transfers their items. This first release is one-way and covers cart creation and transfer only. The guide says updating, deleting, or syncing cart contents between Google and the merchant’s system isn’t supported. Native checkout on Google is a separate API and isn’t required for cart transfer. Participating merchants who meet Google’s onboarding requirements select either option in the UCP integration hub in Merchant Center. Google’s help page says the hub is rolling out gradually in the U.S., with Australia and Canada to follow next year. I covered the hub’s cart transfer option when Google added it in September. The UCP Analytics Reporting dashboard in Merchant Center tracks the checkout funnel from clicks on the Buy button through purchases and cancellations. Google’s Merchant API reference for the same data also lists cart transfer metrics, such as the number of cart transfers and the average cart value at transfer, and describes each as equivalent to a metric in the Merchant Center dashboard. That API reporting is in alpha. None of these pages list a metric for products saved to a cart. Shopify’s support information for its Google AI Mode & Gemini Channel states that Direct Checkout is enabled by default for eligible U.S. Shopify Stores. According to Shopify’s Help Page regarding the Google AI Mode & Gemini Channel, Google Analytics and Custom Pixels will not fire when a customer completes their purchase through the Direct Checkout option. Unfortunately, no information was found about how Universal Cart handles in-cart purchases made from a merchant using the Shopify platform. In addition, we could not determine if in-cart purchases are handled with the same checkout process as purchases completed through Direct Checkout. SEJ contributor Slobodan Manic recently reported on the Default settings for Shopify. Universal Cart allows for a buyer’s shopping list to reside with their account at Google. Checkout can also be performed from the buyer’s shopping list within Google. Two methods are described by Google’s docs to complete a purchase from Universal Cart. The first method of completing a purchase using Universal Cart, known as “Native checkout”, completes the sale via Google. The second method of completing a purchase using Universal Cart, called “Cart Transfer” allows the shopper to create a pre-filled shopping cart upon the shopper’s arrival at the merchant’s website. The UCP sales tracking system tracks both cart transfers and purchases separately. Additionally, the number of purchases tracked by the sales tracking system for Universal Cart includes all completely finished purchases made directly from the shopper’s Universal Cart shopping list. Purchases made after transferring an itemized list of products to a merchant’s website will occur at the merchant’s site. A Shopify store may view whether direct checkout is on via Sales channels > Agentic within the Shopify Admin. Universal Cart is being rolled out in the United States right now before the holiday shopping season begins. The post today does not have a timeline for when YouTube or Gmail will be available, both services Google mentioned they will support later. As long as merchants have been granted access to the UCP integration hub they should continue to see buy click activity, purchase activity, and cart transfer on the analytics tab. A Wealth of Common Sense Posted October 15, 2026 by Ben Carlson A reader asks: Ben has done a good job putting stock market concentration into context for me over the years. I’ve held onto my index funds despite the top 10 holdings becoming a much larger piece of the pie every year. I would be lying though if I said I’m not worried about AI being the ONE BIG TRADE. I’m not a fan of timing the market and going to cash (even with t-bills yielding 4%) so what’s the best way to hedge the concentrated AI trade? How can I diversify but still take risk? People have been worried about stock market concentration for the better part of a decade. I first wrote about it back in 2018. But concentration in the S&P 500 has accelerated this decade. Michael created this chart that shows the relative market cap of the 5 biggest stocks versus the rest of the index over time: Ten years ago the 5 biggest names were worth as much as the bottom 225 stocks. Today the top 5 is worth the same as the bottom 434 stocks. The mega caps just keep getting bigger. You can see how the share of the top 10 stocks has changed in the past 50 years or so: The top 10 stocks have made up somewhere in the range of 20-25% of the index since 1980. Now it’s 40%. That’s a massive jump in the 2020s. You basically have to go back to the 1950s and 1960s for this level of concentration. While it is true that other country stock markets are even more concentrated than the United States, those other countries don’t make up two-thirds of the global equity market capitalization. The 10 biggest stocks in the S&P 500 are currently worth more than $28 trillion. Every single stock in the top 10 now sports a market cap with four commas. The hard part is that you could be worried about concentration while the biggest companies just keep getting bigger. The government doesn’t show any interest in breaking up these companies. Why would they? Consumers love using their products. It’s certainly possible that all of this AI capex will create a situation where the rich get richer and concentration is the new normal. It’s important to remember that the top 10 stocks account for 40% of market cap but 40% of profits as well. It’s also possible we have a nasty bear market that levels the playing field. You can see from Michael’s chart above that concentration fell sharply during the lost decade of the 2000s when the stock market crashed twice. Concentrated markets are a hallmark of bull markets. If the bull market ends, that could change things. The good news for people who are worried about the one big AI trade is that it’s never been easier to diversify than it is today. There are more fund options. The fees are lower. There are more tax efficient options. I don’t know how this will all play out but allow me to take a stab at how things could look if and when the AI trade falls apart: The S&P 500 would fall but the Nasdaq 100 would likely get hit even harder. The top 10 stocks in the Nasdaq 100 make up almost 50% of the total. Bonds would finally earn their keep from a combination of high starting yields and falling interest rates. My guess is that rates would come down fairly quickly if all the AI capex spending slows. That’s good news for bonds and other interest rate sensitive strategies. I also think foreign developed stock markets will do relatively well, especially places like Europe because those markets have a much smaller allocation to tech stocks. Plus basically all of the AI spending is coming from the U.S. The dollar would probably fall if they pull back on AI capex which would be great for foreign stocks from the perspective of a U.S. investor. Most strategies that break from a market cap weighting will likely help you diversify as well. Let’s look at some examples to see why this could be the case from a sector perspective. This is the current sector breakdown for the Vanguard Europe ETF versus the S&P 500: Now look at S&P 500 sector weightings versus the S&P Dividend ETF: And the Vanguard Value ETF: The one thing these funds all have in common is they’re more diversified by sector and have far less exposure to tech stocks.  Here’s a look at the top 10 stocks by weight in each of these funds: There is far less concentration in these other strategies. I’m not saying you have to invest in these funds specifically. There are many different diversifiers that would probably work if AI goes belly up — dividend stocks, value stocks, quality stocks, low vol stocks, bonds, REITs, etc. If the AI trade goes wrong and it leads to a stock market crash I’m not sure how more diversified, fundamentally-driven strategies would hold up. But I do think the last lost decade is probably instructive in terms of asset classes that were left behind coming back into vogue. Diversification is the only rational solution for worries about stock market concentration. Alternatively, you could just stay in index funds and continue letting the market pick the winners for you. Another reader asks: For over half the year the ‘impressive 493’ led the S&P higher while the Lag 7 underperformed. Everyone celebrated breadth. Now the Mag 7 has once again taken the lead and everyone is ringing alarm bells about concentration risk again. Doesn’t this market YTD show the value of owning the index rather than the problems of owning it? This is a fair point too. Look at the performance this year of the S&P 500 vs. the Mag 7 and the S&P 493 (which is ex-Mag 7): They all basically ended up in the same place through the end of September. You just had a much bumpier ride in the Mag 7. If you’re worried about concentration risk the answer is to diversify your holdings. But completely moving away from the gigantic tech companies is also a big bet. You could be right by going all in on AI stocks or you could be right to avoid AI stocks completely. I don’t like the idea of going to either extreme because it opens you up to the possibility of big-time regret. By Andrew Paul    					Published				  					Oct 15, 2026 2:23 PM EDT				  Marine biologists are sounding the alarm on behalf of the Galápagos Islands’ marine iguana (Amblyrhynchus cristatus). Without tightened regulations on the often abused exotic pet trade, researchers warn that a recent “strange uptick” in illegal animal trafficking combined with this season’s Super El Niño is further endangering the already vulnerable reptiles living on the Eastern Pacific archipelago. “They are already shrinking in size and facing mass mortality, either by starvation or by trying to swim longer distances in search of food,” Juan José Alava, a marine ecotoxicologist at Canada’s Simon Fraser University, explained in a recent letter published in Science. The marine iguana family encompasses at least 11 known subspecies, each specially evolved to live on the Galápagos Islands. They are the only reptiles in the world capable of foraging underwater for macroalgae, which makes up the majority of their diet. Although iguana colonies remain relatively stable, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) still lists them as Vulnerable due to predators, mounting pollution issues, and cyclical El Niño events. Ten of the 11 recognized subspecies are also locally classified as either Critically Endangered or Endangered. Sale of iguanas is banned under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), but a recent uptick in illegal trafficking along with increasingly dramatic climate shifts is adding more stress to the situation. Ecuadorian authorities have caught people attempting to smuggle iguanas multiple times this year. In May, officials discovered at least a dozen animals inside handbags at an airport that were bound for illegal markets. Law enforcement found another 32 tied up inside a suitcase intended for similar buyers in August. Many trafficked iguanas won’t survive the stress and rough handling, but even rescued reptiles face challenges. Because subspecies are evolved to live on specific islands, ecologists must test each rescued iguana’s DNA to determine where to return them. Smuggling hasn’t been seen within the Galápagos Marine Reserve itself, but Alava and his colleagues theorize that smugglers are capturing iguanas near Ecuador’s coastal shorelines. Traffickers then obtain CITES permits that falsely declare the reptiles are captive bred in other nations, even though no such authorized facilities actually exist. Often, smugglers are only engaged in the industry out of financial necessity or coercion. “Artisinal fishing communities from Galapagos and coastal Ecuador, who are facing severe socioeconomic hardship and expanding organized crime activities, may feel pressured to participate in this international black market,” the letter’s authors wrote. Conservationists are now urging a multifaceted approach to protect the animals. CITES representatives need to close existing permit loopholes, while the Ecuadorian government should focus on simultaneously breaking up organized crime and providing economic aid to struggling communities. “Maintaining global ocean observing systems is essential, and extreme marine event forecasting and response capabilities are improving,” the authors wrote. “But responsibility and action remain fragmented across environmental [organizations], fisheries, and emergency management, and public health agencies.” 2026 Popular Science Home of the Future Awards 39 products that will improve your everyday life. Chinese smartphone brand OnePlus has had some interesting phones in its portfolio, and lately the company seems to be really pushing the envelope on the battery front. In fact, the company's OnePlus 15 is considered the Android phone with the best battery life in 2026. However, if you are someone who likes to draw, doodle, or just jot down your thoughts the old-fashioned way, the company's portfolio is pretty limited when it comes to phones with stylus support. The OnePlus Open is the only phone from the company that can work with a stylus. Interestingly, the company doesn't mention the stylus support anywhere in the OnePlus Open marketing, official specifications, or on the product page. As a result, the stylus support has become kind of a hidden feature of the phone. Notably, the phone isn't even compatible with OnePlus's own tablet stylus called Stylo, and you need the Oppo Pen if you want a OnePlus Open-compatible stylus. The Oppo Pen is sold as an official accessory to the Oppo Find N3 – the same phone on which the OnePlus Open is based — and the Oppo Find N2. Although OnePlus doesn't explicitly announce this stylus support, the company did confirm in a statement to Android Central that the Oppo Pen can indeed connect with the OnePlus Open. The same has also been checked by Reddit users, and the Oppo Pen works pretty seamlessly with the OnePlus Open and enables features that you wouldn't otherwise get. The Oppo Pen can work with both the inner display and the outer display of the OnePlus Open, and when you pair it with the phone, it might trigger a firmware update to enable all the related features. You can double-tap the stylus button to take a screenshot, use the stylus as a camera remote, or draw a line from the top-right corner of the screen to launch the Notes app. Plus, you can tap the stylus button to switch between tools, and there is support for palm rejection and 4,096 levels of pressure sensitivity. The overall consensus on Reddit is that the Oppo Pen works without issues with the OnePlus foldable, with at least one person even comparing it to the Apple Pencil. One drawback called out by a user is the battery performance, which they hoped was better. The Oppo Pen comes with a charging dock that you use with a USB-C wall adapter to juice up the stylus. Unfortunately, although the OnePlus Open was officially introduced in the U.S. in October 2023, it's pretty hard to buy one right now. If you go to the OnePlus online store to purchase the Open, it simply says, "Sorry, this product is not available to purchase in your region temporarily." So ordering from the OnePlus online store is out of the question. However, it isn't even available as new at Amazon, Best Buy, or any other reputable store. The only place that seems to be stocking it is Cell2Get, which doesn't have a good TrustPilot rating or reviews from folks on Reddit. That said, if you don't mind a pre-owned model, there are units available as part of Amazon Renewed and as refurbished on places like Best Buy, Swappa, and eBay. Remember, you have to be pretty careful when buying pre-owned foldable smartphones, as they are more fragile than traditional phones. More importantly, remember that OnePlus has exited the U.S. market, and while it will continue to service and update the existing devices, it might be trickier to get spare parts and replacements. The Oppo Pen, on the other hand, was never launched in the U.S. and, as a result, you can't officially buy it in the country. The only way to get it is through eBay or another store that imports it from China or another country. This also means you will have to pay a premium to get the stylus.

Handheld gaming PCs require a delicate balance of portability, performance, and price. The good ones, like the Steam Deck OLED, can hit two out of the three. The ROG Xbox Ally X20 doesn't change much from last year's Xbox Ally X, except for an OLED screen and a few smart design changes. Oh, and it's wildly more expensive at $1,300. Under its new transparent black exterior and fancy gold trim, the Ally X20 has the same AMD Ryzen CPU, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage as last year's ROG Xbox Ally X. The stunning 7.4-inch OLED is the main draw, making it a close rival to the Steam Deck OLED. The Ally X20 has two USB-C ports, one of which supports USB4 and is Thunderbolt compatible, so it'll work with a compatible dock and external SSD. The other port supports up to USB 3.2 Gen 2, meaning both support charging and video output if you want to connect to a monitor. You also get a 3.5mm headphone jack and a microSD Express card reader (an upgrade over Ally X's UHS-II reader) for expanding storage. Older microSD cards still work, though you'll need an Express card to take advantage of the faster connection. In last year's ROG Xbox Ally X review, we praised its performance, but found that Windows 11 and its hefty size complicated the experience. Many of those issues remain, even if the X20 improves comfort and grip. The question remains whether the OLED is worth the $300 price hike. The biggest reason to consider the Ally X20 is its gorgeous 7.4-inch OLED screen, compared with the Ally and Ally X's 7-inch LCD. The resolution and refresh rate stay the same: 1920x1080 at 120Hz, with slightly more screen real estate. I've been playing a lot of "Gears of War: E-Day," a surprisingly good game that shows off what this OLED can do. Dark Locust tunnels and abandoned subway stations highlight the display's deep blacks, while twilight and daytime scenes show off its rich colors and HDR-enhanced brightness.  The display supports HDR peaks of up to 1,400 nits and FreeSync Premium Pro to keep gameplay smooth. With the same hardware as last year's model, the screen has to justify a big chunk of that $300 premium. For me, the difference is hard to ignore: Going from LCD to OLED makes familiar games look noticeably better. It doesn't come close: The bump in color and brightness OLED offers in comparison to LCD is like nothing else. Games like "Hades 2" are where you can come to appreciate how much the colors pop. The Ally X20 celebrates ROG's (Asus Republic of Gamers) 20th anniversary with a translucent black shell and gold accents. I'm always a sucker for translucent designs that reveal the internal components. However, I would have preferred an alternate colorway to choose from, since I really did like the white of last year's Ally X that gave it a more premium look. The most noticeable change is one you feel under your fingertips. The bumpers and triggers have been slightly reshaped and the grips are rubberized. The end result feels like you're holding an oversized Xbox controller, which makes sense considering all the Xbox branding and partnership. This is especially important because this thing is heavy: Weighing in at 756 grams, it's 41 grams heavier than the Ally X, and 116 grams heavier than the Steam Deck OLED. The improved grips are welcome, but you're holding up one rather hefty handheld. Another interesting feature is the transforming D-pad. Lift it slightly and rotate it to switch it between four-way and eight-way directional inputs. It's useful if looking to dive into matches of "Street Fighter" or "Tekken" on the bus. I dove into some bouts in "Marvel vs. Capcom Fighting Collection: Arcade Classics" and found the D-pad to be mostly serviceable. If you're someone who gets a little fatigued holding up your phone or tablet for too long, the Ally X20 might end up feeling like you're holding a barbell above your face. Despite its Xbox branding, the Ally X20 is a Windows 11 gaming PC, and that flexibility is most of the appeal. It lets you install games from different PC storefronts, and basically anything you can do on a Windows PC, you can do on the Ally X20. A dedicated Xbox button lets you switch from the Xbox app to a Windows desktop right on the fly. While it was nice to be able to install games from the Epic Games Store, Steam, GOG and Xbox, the initial setup was a bit of a headache, since it used the 7-inch touchscreen to add your credentials and deal with driver updates. The best way to deal with it is to connect a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse and do it the old fashioned way. Another slight annoyance with Windows 11 on handheld is that some games' graphics settings defaulted to whatever I had on PC, like games from the Epic Store. Every time I played "Control Resonant" from my gaming PC, and wanted to continue on the Ally X20, I had to manually change graphics settings each time I loaded up the game. Navigating the Xbox app, which is instantly launched every time you turn on the system (or "Xbox mode," as ROG calls it), its controller-friendly interface was a breeze to use. Game Pass is a huge part of the X20's pitch, particularly if you already subscribed and want a portable way to play those Xbox first-party games. If you're not part of the Xbox ecosystem, or don't plan to be, those features are going to be wasted on you. The Ally X20 keeps the Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme CPU, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD from last year's model. Considering how well the Ryzen-powered handheld performed in the Ally X, the X20 isn't vastly different. For the sake of comparison, I ran the same games we tested the Ally X on, in addition to a couple of newer titles like "Gears of War: E-Day" and "Control Resonant," to see how much the Ally X20 performed in both Turbo and Performance modes. Here are the Geekbench scores: Single-Core Score: 2814 Multi-Core Score: 11980 OpenCL Score: 39023 The Ally X20 is a powerful piece of hardware averaging around 30-32 fps in games like "Gears of War: E-Day" and "Control Resonant" on low to medium graphical presets in Turbo Mode (25W). "Cyberpunk 2077" ran surprisingly well, hitting around 43 fps in the Steam Deck graphical preset. Even though performance is roughly the same, the improved cooling was something I noticed after about an hour of gaming where the console ran cooler than the Steam Deck OLED. The 80Wh battery, combined with the OLED screen, provides a decent enough battery depending on which performance setting you're working with. More demanding AAA games will get 2-3 hours of playtime, which you'd want to run in Turbo mode for the best framerate. I was able to get around 2 hours for "Resident Evil Requiem," and three hours for "Star Wars Zero Company." Less taxing games will get you between 6-8 hours of battery life. "Final Fantasy Tactics: The Ivalice Chronicles" split the difference at 6 hours and 34 minutes, and got nearly 8 hours of "Blood Dungeon" in Silent Mode. The Ally X20 improves the parts of a handheld that you interact with constantly: The screen, grips, and controls. Those changes deserve more credit than a new color scheme alone, and the OLED gives me something additional to appreciate. However, at $1,300, the Ally X20 sets a high bar. Last year's Xbox Ally had the same processor, RAM, capacity, storage, and battery for $300 less. While the X20 looks more appealing, it's tough to recommend if you already own an Ally X. That said, if you're in the market for a powerful handheld gaming PC, but not looking to spend over $2,000 on a Windows 11 handheld like the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ or the Lenovo Legion Go Gen 2; the Ally X20 feels more like the best Goldilocks option. The OLED screen is a nice addition to a handheld console with decent battery life and a mostly versatile operating system. The Ally X20 is perfect for anyone with large game libraries across multiple PC gaming storefronts, assuming you want to handle something that's a bit more chunky than a Steam Deck. The ROG Xbox Ally X20 launches on October 15 for $1,299.99. There's also the ROG Xbox Ally X20 console bundle, which includes the Ally X20, Pelican carrying case, and the ROG XREAL R1 Edition 20 gaming glasses for $2,499.99.

Looking at prices for brand-new PC components, it's difficult to see how someone on a budget could put together a new rig capable of high framerates at 1080p, let alone 1440p gaming. Everything is significantly more expensive than it was a year ago, but that doesn't mean it's impossible to put together a decent machine. The pre-owned market was the best way for budget builders to make an entry into PC gaming before the memory crisis, and it still is today. It'll take some patience and a little bit of trust, but it's more doable than you might expect. It's all a matter of priorities There aren't as many folks upgrading from AM4 to AM5 or from an older Intel platform to a newer one, but there are still plenty of people trying to get a few extra bucks for their old CPU, motherboard and RAM. Selling them piece by piece can be tedious, so you'll find a lot of listings on eBay for combos that have all three in the same box. Memory is the main reason why building a PC is so expensive right now, and trying to find someone selling theirs in a bundle is the best way to get your hands on some. There are tons of listings that have been sold in the last 30 days for Ryzen 5 5600X, Ryzen 7 5800X, and Intel Core i7-10700K bundles that include some memory and a motherboard, and they're usually going anywhere from $250 to $400. At that higher end, it is possible to find a newer platform; I saw an AM5 board with a Ryzen 5 7600 for $400, which isn't an excellent deal, but it's certainly better than paying the brand-new tax. The Zen 3 chip seemed like the best choice at the moment, but boy do I have regrets The graphics card is at the heart of every gaming PC, and when you're trying to build a 1440p-capable machine for under $1,000, it's also where things start to get pretty tight. Between Nvidia, AMD, and Intel, there are only a handful of realistic options. Of the Radeon candidates, the RX 9060 XT 16GB is probably the best bang-for-buck card, but it's also on the more expensive side, coming in at just over $500 at the time of writing for the cheapest available option. It's a great 1440p card, and its 16GB of VRAM ensures that it's not going to become a paperweight in the coming years. On the Nvidia side of the fence, it's not much better. The RTX 5060 Ti 16GB is not in the discussion, as its current price makes up nearly three quarters of the entire build. For other RTX options, you're basically limited to the pre-owned market. An RTX 3080 has 10GB of VRAM and is still a great 1440p card, but it's a bit pricy at the moment. Most cards are going for well above $350, but that price seems to be the floor. On Intel there's really only one option, and it's the B580. It's a fringe 1440p card, and at its current somewhat inflated price of $320 at the time of writing, it's a bit expensive when there are better pre-owned options available. All of these cards are capable of 1440p gameplay, some definitely more than others. The "best" components might not be the best choice for your build The power supply is the one part I’d never buy used. You can’t meaningfully test one at home, its wear is invisible, and a failing unit can take other parts with it. A quality 650W to 750W unit leaves headroom for a power-hungry chip like the 10700K and a card like the RX 9060 XT, if that's the route you intend to go. If you do end up buying a pre-owned 3080, you'll need a bit more PSU headroom: 800W and above is what I'd feel good running. Storage is more flexible. A 1TB Gen4 NVMe drive that bottomed out around $55 to $65 in 2024 now runs $100 to $150. Unlike a PSU, though, an SSD’s wear is readable: its SMART data shows how much of its rated endurance has been used. Some combos include a drive, like the Core i7-11700 and Z490 Aorus Ultra bundle that sold for $350 with a 500GB WD NVMe drive. The case and cooler can come from anywhere, as long as the case fits your board and moves air, you're good to go. I'd even try to find these used in your area—cases are the one thing some people will just give away in order to free up some space in their home. Dirt-cheap Xeon workstations can still bring it in gaming  When buying pre-owned PC components, there's always a risk. There's almost never going to be a warranty remaining for the parts you buy from a place like eBay, even if the seller has the original proof-of-payment. The used market absolutely has its fair share of misrepresented listings, bent pins, and RAM that throws errors under load. On a budget this tight, one dud wipes out the savings, but it's not a total diceroll. eBay’s Money Back Guarantee covers items that arrive not as described, even when the seller doesn’t accept returns, as long as you contact the seller within 30 days of the actual or estimated delivery date. A CPU listed as working that won’t boot qualifies. Thirty days is plenty, because the parts this build buys used are the ones you can test thoroughly in an afternoon. Run MemTest86 on the RAM, stress the CPU with OCCT or Cinebench, inspect the socket pins, and check the BIOS version. The parts with real wear mechanisms, like PSU capacitors, GPU fans, and SSD flash, are either bought new or checked through SMART. We want to hear from you. Sony hiked the prices of the PlayStation 5 here in the States, including the Pro, but that hasn't stopped anyone from buying the consoles — more than 95 million PS5s had been sold as of June 2026. But if you were to go shopping for the console in Japan, Sony's domestic market, you'd find it much cheaper. That's even more relevant considering Sony just unveiled a new version of the console, a "Midnight Black" model that's pretty sleek looking (shown below). The caveat? It won't be available outside of Japan, and it's completely region-locked to local PSN accounts — the system language is forced to Japanese and the country settings must match. That's what makes the PlayStation 5 consoles from the region exclusive. As for the Midnight Black model, it's scheduled to launch on November 19, 2026, and will cost ¥55,000 — the equivalent of $350 USD. You might also recognize that day as the official launch date for the next "Grand Theft Auto" installment. The new model is a digital version of the PS5 console with the model number CFI-2200B02S, per PlayStation Japan, and there will be a matching disc drive available separately. This is a nearly identical model to the one released in November 2025, albeit that one was all-white. If you spotted the recent news that PS5 Pro prices have gone through the roof — as high as $1,500 at some retailers — you're probably wishing and hoping Sony releases some cheaper models stateside. Unfortunately, that's not likely to happen, and if new models do become available, they'll probably be priced similarly to the existing stock. If you're still on the fence about getting a PlayStation 5 and don't have one yet, or if you're considering an upgrade to a PS5 Pro from the base model, the current prices are certainly one big reason to shy away. Is it actually worth the high cost? The answer is unequivocally "it depends," and the balance is 50-50. There are just as many reasons why it's not worth it as there are reasons why it is. News also recently broke that Sony sold several patents related to VR tech, which doesn't bode well for the PSVR2. So, if you were grabbing a console for that, you might want to reconsider. There is some potentially good news, however — a light at the end of the tunnel, so to speak. Media outlets are now reporting PS5 physical unit sales are down because of the price hikes. There is a chance, however small, that Sony may lower prices eventually, or may offer sales and promotions to compensate. Then again, when Sony raised the prices in April, it cited "continued pressures" in the market, meaning the rising costs and shortages due to global memory and storage availability. Because of that, no one really knows how long the PlayStation 5 Pro shortage will last, or the related hardware shortages for that matter. It looks like early 2027 would be the earliest those pressures might start to subside. All of this is just to say that it might be quite some time before we see PS5 hardware prices come down to what many would consider reasonable. Granted, Sony is expected to offer some deals for Black Friday and the coming holidays.

TOPICS                      security                    PWNED            The term military intelligence seems like an oxymoron in this case      Welcome, once again, to PWNED, the weekly column where we gawk at organizations that have made serious security mistakes. Normally, we’re talking about businesses or maybe the odd school that messes up, but today we’re writing about a serious IT screwup in the world’s most powerful military. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request. Today’s tale comes from Justin Henkel, the CISO of IT monitoring and service company SolarWinds. Henkel previously worked in IT security for the Air Force and one day in the early 2000s saw a practice that just wouldn’t fly today. Before USB drives became popular, burning CDs with mission data was the modus operandi, and those discs were put in both unclassified and classified systems. “They would write a CD, and then they would take that CD and then put it in a classified system and do the remainder of the mission planning,” Henkel told us. “Then they would take that disc and then put it in the airplane.” Inside the airplane, the data on the CD would help the pilot navigate and contain information about threats they might encounter.  Later, when thumb drives became a thing, pilots used them instead of discs.  “They didn't really think about the overall impact of classified versus unclassified systems,” Henkel said of the pilots. “Using the same device for both, they didn’t understand that you could read and write onto a USB drive with malware. [They were] not really understanding the overall threat picture.” According to Henkel, Air Force personnel would buy their flash drives from local vendors rather than sourcing them from official military contractors. If they were in Afghanistan, those drives could literally come from a store in Kabul. And it wasn’t exactly the equivalent of Best Buy.   “It was more difficult to bring a US-based computer into the nation than it was just to buy local,” he said. “So they were just going out into the local market in Kabul or whatever city that they were out [in]. And I used to do this: go out, make relationships with the local vendors. ‘Hey I need 100 USB sticks.’” Unfortunately, enemies of the US noticed and soon started selling infected USB drives to local vendors in the Middle East. Henkel knew that using a sneakernet with classified systems was a recipe for disaster. It’s just that no one would listen to him. “It was just a shock,” he told us. “I was a young 22-year-old guy, very junior in the overall rank system, trying to tell colonels and majors that what they’re doing is a violation.” In 2008, the US Department of Defense was infected by malware after somebody attached an infected USB flash drive to a laptop with access to US Central Command. The worm, dubbed Agent.BTZ, could collect information from infected computers and communicate with remote servers. A 2016 report from the FBI and DHS attributed the malware to one or more Russian groups.  It took the Pentagon 14 months to scrub it from its systems.  It took this attack for the Pentagon to wise up in 2008 and ban the use of USB drives, instead forcing data transfers to go through more secure systems.
