Of all the options in the survey, “the one problem that you don’t want to be your #1 problem is poor sales,” the asset manager says. “During prior economic contractions, we’ve seen this reading for poor sales tick sharply higher. As shown below, while still relatively low for now, it has begun to tick higher again recently.”  The NFIB index fell to 97.9 in September, from 98.7 in August. “The other major business surveys also generally suggest that activity lost a little momentum towards the end of Q3, likely weighed down by the rebound in global energy prices,” according to Samuel Tombs and Oliver Allen at Pantheon Macroeconomics. (They also note that only 411 companies responded to the survey, down from a level of around 1,200 over a decade ago.) Mark Zandi at Moody’s Analytics thinks the U.S. economy is “vulnerable.” He is especially worried about the labor market: “Monthly payroll growth has averaged around 40,000 over the past year and has been essentially zero when excluding the healthcare sector. Hiring is moribund, hours worked are very low, and while the unemployment rate remains low, that is partly a reflection of declining labor force participation [from increased retirements and low immigration,]” he told Goldman Sachs’ Allison Nathan recently. In addition, he’s concerned that higher rates being demanded by the Fed and the bond market could derail AI capex spending. “AI capex is also vulnerable as a higher cost of capital makes investment more expensive and falling valuations make it harder to raise the capital necessary to sustain the current pace of the AI buildout,” he says. “If rates remain at these levels or higher for longer than a quarter or two, AI could become the part of the economy that breaks.” That scenario—interest rates higher for longer—appears to be shaping up. The consumer price index for September came in at 3.7%, up from 3.4% the previous month and ahead of analysts’ expectations. The Fed may feel compelled to act by raising rates further. “Inflation is cooking with gas,” Jamie Cox of the Harris Financial Group told Fortune in an email. “It is abundantly clear where the inflation impulse originates, but two wars need to end before we get any relief. The Federal Reserve made the mistake of calling Covid-era inflation transitory, and now it appears they are set to make the same mistake in reverse on the energy supply shock.” Pimco’s Tiffany Wilding was equally alarmed: “This is not a good data point for the Federal Reserve, whose committee members had been signaling they were not likely to raise interest rates later this month. After the [CPI] report was published, markets priced in a 50 percent chance that the central bank would raise rates again in October.” Traders decided they hate tech stocks in the last 24 hours, driving a global wave of selling. The tech-heavy South Korean KOSPI index fell 8% and at one point triggered a halt in trading. Nasdaq futures were down 1.03% this morning, signalling that the bloodletting may continue after the markets open in New York. CoreWeave lost 15.46% yesterday and sank a further 5.89% overnight; Oracle was down 8.83%, and lost another 1.57% in post-market trading. Chipmakers suffered declines across the board. My garage shelf holds more Ryobi batteries than I ever run at once. Most came inside tool kits, and a few I bought on price before I understood what separated one pack from another. I've written about how the battery became the real investment in my Ryobi setup, and that lesson got sharper in August when Ryobi reshuffled its 18V lineup.  The old standard packs are on their way out, the teal High Performance line now carries the plain 18V ONE+ Lithium name, and EDGE sits above it. So I sorted every 18V and 40V pack I own into two piles: the ones I'd pay for again and the ones I'd leave on the peg. If I could rebuy only one 18V battery, it would be the teal 4.0Ah (PBP004). It spends most weekends on my circular saw and moves between the impact driver and oscillating multi-tool during basement projects. Under load, the saw holds its speed through a full rip instead of slowing halfway down the board. Weight matters as much as output. Overhead work with an impact driver gets tiring fast, and this pack keeps the tool balanced in a way the 6.0Ah can't. It's the pack behind most of what I described when High Performance batteries rescued my budget Ryobi tools. It lists at $129, but Home Depot's battery promotions cut it close to half often enough that I've never paid full price. You can use your power tools batteries on more devices and gadgets than you think.  The 6.0Ah (PBP007) goes on anything that runs continuously rather than in bursts. Its most useful job has nothing to do with woodworking. My Dyson V8 runs on Ryobi packs through an inexpensive battery adapter, and on this one the vacuum outlasts its stock Dyson battery by a comfortable margin. It also pairs well with my heat gun, which pulls power for minutes at a stretch. A smaller pack can get it through a job, but the 6.0Ah finishes without a return trip to the charger, and that's what I'm paying for. The trade-off is bulk. I pull it off handheld tools once the long task wraps up. For most households, one of these plus one 4.0Ah covers nearly every 18V job. I bought the standard 4.0Ah (PBP005) because it cost $30 less than the teal pack hanging beside it. It still charges and works, but on any tool with real motor load, it performs like a heavier version of a kit battery. Ryobi seems to agree. Starting in August 2026, the standard tier is being phased out at Home Depot. The former High Performance batteries now carry the 18V ONE+ Lithium label in 2.0Ah, 4.0Ah, and 6.0Ah sizes, each with IntelliCell electronics and Cool-Core heat management. The old High Performance EDGE packs become Lithium EDGE, sold in 4.0Ah, 8.0Ah, and 12.0Ah. The pack I regret is disappearing, and the pack I'd rebuy just became the baseline. If you find a leftover standard 4.0Ah on clearance, pass unless the discount is steep and it's headed for a drill. My 1.5Ah and 2.0Ah packs all arrived bundled, and they still do useful work. One stays on the drill for pilot holes and light assembly, where a lighter tool is easier to control. Another rides on the tire inflator, which tops off a tire in a few minutes and never asks for more. I just won't pay retail for one. A compact falters the moment it meets a circular saw or sander, so buying one outright means spending money on the least flexible pack in the system. If you need a small battery for overhead or tight-space work, the new 2.0Ah Lithium is the only compact I'd consider, since it carries the same IntelliCell electronics as its larger siblings. My 40V side runs a string trimmer, leaf blower, hedge trimmer, and edger across 2.5 acres, fed by 4Ah, 6Ah, and 8Ah packs. Only the 6Ah would make it back into my cart. The 4Ah handles the hedge trimmer and edger, which finish their jobs quickly. On the string trimmer, it gives out before I've worked the full property line, and that means a walk back to the garage and a wait on the charger. The 8Ah has the opposite problem. It keeps the blower going well past the driveway, but hanging that much weight off a trimmer for an hour wears on my shoulders. It makes more sense on a self-propelled mower, where the machine carries the load. The 6Ah lands in between. It gets the trimmer through a full lap of the yard and runs the blower long enough for fall cleanup without making either tool miserable to hold. If you're starting a 40V collection, two 6Ah packs beat one of each size.  Every pack I'd rebuy sits in the middle of its lineup. The 4.0Ah and 6.0Ah High Performance batteries cover my 18V tools, and the 40V 6Ah handles the yard. Ryobi's rebrand also simplifies the 18V decision: the standard tier is going away, and the Lithium label now marks the packs worth owning.  Save EDGE for bench tools and other heavy draws where runtime beats weight. Before you spend $200 or more on the biggest pack Ryobi makes, read why the largest battery isn't always an upgrade. A pair of mid-size packs will likely serve you better. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. The Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL find themselves at something of a crossroads. The Californian company made a viable stake in the smartphone market with its flagship phones impressing with powerful camera systems, a deeply ingrained native Google ecosystem, stellar build quality, and a clean, bloat-free Android user experience. All of these core points are true for the latest handset in the lineup; however, with Google scrapping the cheaper 128GB option, this year's model effectively comes in $100 / £100 / €100 more expensive while offering 4GB less RAM. You're paying more for less due to the ongoing RAM crisis/global memory shortage, which makes this device feel like a hard sell despite its notable improvements. Starting at $1,099 / £1,079 / €1,199 for the 256GB Pro or $1,299 / £1,279 / €1,399 for the Pro XL variant, we're long beyond the days of Google undercutting its competition. The Pixel 11 Pro is steeply priced alongside devices like the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra and the iPhone 18 Pro. Given the chokehold that Apple has as the primary market shareholder in the US, and Samsung being the biggest Android-based phone manufacturer, the Pixel 11 Pro and XL variants are fighting a tough uphill battle, not for dominance, but for relevance. Google's Pixel 11 Pro impresses with its iPhone-like approach to build quality, its pleasingly straightforward operating system, and a surprisingly useful suite of Gemini-backed AI functionality. With that said, it's also far from the most powerful smartphone on the market, and this year's so-so features, combined with less RAM and a price increase for the cheapest model, make it difficult to recommend over the still-excellent Pixel 10 Pro or Pixel 10 Pro XL. The Google Pixel 11 Pro features exceptional build quality, a great multi-camera array, and a slick bloat-free Android experience. It could be the ultimate Android smartphone, but it’s slightly let down by a higher price and minimal improvements over its predecessor. I've been using the Google Pixel 11 Pro as my daily driver, and the main reason I'm considering it over its competitors is its battery life. Intelligent optimizations of the new Tensor G6 processor have enabled Google to push the respectable 4,850 mAh battery (or 5,115 mAh on the 11 Pro XL) far beyond what's typically expected for a handset's lifespan between charges. It's down ever-so-slightly from the Pixel 10 Pro's 4,870 mAh battery, although that's ultimately inconsequential given just how long this device lasts day-to-day. Google claims the Pixel 11 Pro can last for over 30 hours of playback under moderate use, and my testing confirms this. For more casual use cases, such as web browsing, instant messaging, and other lower-impact use cases, I barely noticed the battery percentage tick down at all and was only really reaching for the included USB-C every three days or so. The battery options from the stock Android experience are also greatly appreciated; right from the "Battery and charging" menu, you can see the battery's health, add a widget to test it, get a full breakdown of which apps used the most juice with the screen time and background consumption, and also run diagnostic reports. There are preset options for a battery draining too quickly, the phone being too warm, a charging issue, or you can report something specific, and the Gemini Nano will run that test for you. The same level of hardware monitoring is also available for charging the Pixel 11 Pro. By default, "charging optimization" is enabled, which automatically completes the chemical charging process at 100%, preventing unnecessary wear and tear on the battery over the long term. You can also limit it to 80%, which is said to better preserve a lithium-ion battery over months and years, following the 80/20 rule. High stress at 100% and instability at 0%, so using that 60% battery range is best for preservation. There's also an Extreme Charging Mode that kicks in when the phone drops to under 50%. It pauses all background activity and automatically regulates temperatures to get you up to speed without risking thermal throttling, provided you're plugged into a proper 30W brick. Everyday performance of the Google Pixel 11 Pro is remarkably slick and fast. As touched upon above, there's (thankfully) no custom Android wrapper here, such as Samsung's One UI or OnePlus' OxygenOS. That means no unneeded bloatware, keeping your storage clean, and ensuring you have the final say over what you install and where it is. Android phone manufacturers tend to move certain options around or bury settings deep in menus. You won't have that problem with this phone; it's straightforward to navigate. It should be instantly familiar to anyone who's used an Android phone before, but not too off-putting for any iPhone users who are only used to the uniform nature of iOS. As you'd hope really, Google's integrated ecosystem works well on its own tech of its own phone. Where you'll notice the limits of the Google Pixel 11 Pro's performance compared to its similarly priced rivals is in the raw horsepower of the Tensor G6. That's due in part to how the G6 is constructed: it is dominated by its fifth-generation TPU, which runs Gemini Nano's on-device AI functions. This Tensor Processing Unit also powers Pixel's trademark high-end computational photography. The result here is a chip that's exceptional at one particular thing, AI, but falls short in the arms race against the likes of the Snapdragon 8 Elite Series, Apple A19 Bionic, and other top-end chips from other phones crossing the four-digit mark in 2026. It's something of an architectural trade-off. The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 found in today's smartphones, such as the Samsung Galaxy S26, Xiaomi 17 Series, OnePlus 15, Honor Magic 8 Series, and others, primarily puts the 8-core custom Oryon CPU and high-performance Adreno GPU ahead of the Hexagon NPU powering the AI functionality. Google flips the script, but the Pixel 11 Pro ultimately pays the price in terms of raw horsepower. This is most notable when gaming. If you're someone who enjoys demanding software from a handset, then the Pixel 11 Pro isn't going to be for you. The 7-core Arm C1-Pro CPU and PowerVR CXTP GPU are good enough for moderate gaming, but the phone struggles under load. I noticed this especially with Fortnite when forcing 60 FPS mode for the Blitz Royale and Battle Royale modes. Even when the game auto-detected the right settings to use, setting everything to Low and disabling any intensive graphics options, stuttering was common. Not only was I contending with micro-stuttering and slowdown from the game, even with a fresh install, but the device was routinely dropping frames, making things basically unplayable. It was a slightly more palatable experience when locking 30 FPS at a maximum, but the trade-off there is the smoothness of a competitive game. It would have been different if it were rock-solid, but it wasn't. It's, unfortunately, a similar story with PUBG Mobile, which hovers at an inconsistent 30 FPS. Things are better with more optimized mobile games, chiefly the older Call of Duty Mobile and the recently released Rainbow Six Mobile. The former has been available since 2019, so any respectable mobile phone has no difficulty maintaining a rock-solid 60 FPS for its suite of mobile-friendly multiplayer modes. Siege's mobile companion isn't quite as consistent when played on the Pixel 11 Pro, but it's night-and-day performance-wise when compared to Fortnite and PUBG; I was averaging between 45 and 60 FPS with the game locked at 60 FPS and the graphics auto-detected to the High preset. There were occasional framerate drops for explosions, reinforcing walls, and close-quarters firefights with multiple enemies; however, it rarely ever dipped below 30 FPS, the playable standard for a tactical shooter like that. The premium build quality and design language of the Pixel 11 Pro extend to its 6.3-inch OLED display, with impressive near-4K-nit peak brightness and extensive HDR support. Media playback is exceptional on this phone. The proclaimed (seemingly) infinite 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio means the colors pop while the deep, inky blacks are bottomless. Throughout my time with the phone, I primarily watched TV shows like Cobra Kai, binge-watched Valorant (and other gaming) content on YouTube, and played games in my downtime. Without question, this is the nicest display I've ever seen on a smartphone, and one of the consistently brightest panels of any portable device I've ever had hands-on with ever. The older Pixel 10 Pro was somewhat revolutionary for reaching 3,300-nit peak brightness. I have to commend the new Pixel 11 Pro for going a step beyond with a new high of 3,600 nits, making it one of the brightest and best displays on the market today, especially in the West (China's Honor phones reach as high as 6,000 nits under certain conditions). It's not just the standard content either; HDR has seen a noticeable bump to 2,400 nits of brightness, up from 2,200 nits the year before. If you struggle to see your phone screen in broad daylight, or want an exceptional-looking screen with no compromises, then Google's flagship delivers here. It's a bright display, but it's also smooth and quick where it needs to be. Backed by LTPO (Low-Temperature Polycrystalline Oxide) technology, the Pixel 11 Pro's screen dynamically refreshes, dropping as low as 1Hz to 10Hz for anything static, but ramping up to as fast as 120Hz for gaming or scrolling. The battery only works as hard as it has to, and the display compensates accordingly. Now, 120Hz is about as quick as you need a smartphone to be. Few modern games on the Android platform can take advantage of a framerate above 60, and most social and productivity apps are geared to being as efficient on power as possible by dropping unneeded frames. If you hate AI, then you're going to want a different mobile phone in 2026. Google isn't shy about pushing its Gemini platform across its ecosystem, and that extends to the Pixel 11 Pro, more so than last year's device. While the Pixel 10 Pro was primarily marketed on its deep Gemini integration, specifically through the Gemini Nano (or fully localized) variant, things have been kicked up a notch with the new handset. Gemini Intelligence can now be found in more than 40 apps and tools, with highlights including Rambler, to transcribe and improve how you speak into the phone, eliminating natural stutters, and also (most pressingly) now with what the company is calling Magic Capture. Don't let the marketing gimmicks fool you. Magic Capture is essentially just Apple's Live Photos feature with an automatic "best take" still. Google claims the Gemini models analyze "around 400 frames" of a video to produce a 12MP image and can even crop and unblur things using its generative AI functionality, so that you never miss a moment. It's a novel idea, and if it were to work more consistently, I would be all for it. Magic Capture is a huge part of the advertising campaign, said to automatically highlight those blink-and-you'll-miss-it moments for fast-moving pets and the like. Well, in my testing of getting photos from a few five-second clips when photographing my playful Belgian Malinois or my Degus, animals who all hate to stay still when I'm trying to test cameras, the results were just OK. They looked like still images taken from a video clip rather than the full, uncompressed photo I wanted. A similar thing happened when I used another brief clip of my Degus hanging out in the hammock. It's situational, and better than nothing, but far from revolutionary. Check out the comparison shots below. AI is better elsewhere, though. As someone who uses Gemini often, I found the home screen prompts to ask questions, share video feeds, or engage with Gemini Live to be great touches. As you can imagine, the native Gemini integration on new Pixels feels much more seamless on the Pixel 11 Pro than on an iPhone. Instead of forcing you to stay inside a dedicated app, Gemini functions as an unobtrusive system overlay, ready to assist via voice or touch at any time. You can also share your screen or stream live video to give the AI contextual awareness for complex tasks. While Gemini Nano efficiently handles localized background tasks, the cloud-based model shines because the phone's entire operating system is built around it. Google's commitment to computational photography and processing made the Pixels among the best smartphones for taking photos, and that's just as true with the Pixel 11 Pro. The triple rear camera system is incredible, simply put. The device benefits from a 50MP main wide-angle lens, a 48MP Ultrawide lens, and a 48MP Telephoto lens with 5x optical zoom. Regardless of lighting conditions, the results are incredible. It's all thanks to the Quad PD sensor, which offers substantially greater light sensitivity than the Pixel 10 Pro, all in a sleeker camera bar on the rear. It's backed by the Tensor G6's Real Tone engine, which forgoes the typical filters and smoothing of smartphone cameras in favor of a dedicated, hardware-accelerated solution. Specifically, it's the Image Signal Processor on the 5th-generation TPU that does that heavy lifting. Real-time identification of elements within a frame that are individually processed. This combines everything from automated white balance algorithms to auto-exposure tuning and proper color processing. Complex backlighting, highlights, and shadows can look better here than on any other phone, even a frontrunner like the iPhone 17 Pro Max, despite Apple's zero-latency, rawer hardware being technically superior. When it comes to point-and-shoot immediacy, the Pixel 11 Pro is genuinely hard to beat, and it's powered by enough handy software to give most average users the edge. In my testing with the Pixel 11 Pro's rear camera system, I was most impressed by how sharp and detailed an image of the same object could look at 5x optical zoom as with 1x and 2x. This was most apparent when I was taking shots of my guitars and motorcycles, with the finer details of strings and dirty, mechanical hardware being perfectly preserved. There's no native 10x zoom lens; however, the 10x option on the phone takes what the 5x Telephoto can do and smartly crops inwards before applying digital processing, yielding surprisingly decent results. I looked hard for signs of lighting mismatches, artificial smoothing, or a loss of focus, which typically give away a partially generated image, but to my surprise, it looked consistently good to my eye. I can't imagine the 10x zoom will be many people's go-to, but it held up better than I expected. Speaking of a generated picture, the Pixel 11 Pro features a 120x Super Zoom, which takes what's achieved from the 10x zoom and magnifies it significantly. The Tensor G6 chip really does the heavy lifting here, taking more of a reference image from what you point at it rather than cleaning up what's immediately in front of the viewfinder. It's less "AI-enhanced" and more "mostly AI," as computational photography is truly heavily slanted toward one side. For best results, you should aim to use this feature on something simple and static for a far-away shot, and with as much natural light as possible. In darker environments, noise is introduced, and the G6 can't quite always make a clean cut. It's the same idea as Samsung's "Space Zoom," which made the headlines back in 2020, promising up to 100x zoom and letting you "take a photo" of the moon. Well, AI has caught up a lot since then. Is it authentic? No. Will most people use this feature more than once or twice out of sheer novelty? Again, it's unlikely, but the option is there for you to try out. Speaking of camera tech, Night Sight is awesome. The Pixel 11 Pro is exceptional for low-light photography owing to that vastly upgraded sensor and the added power of the G6's ISP. To properly test it out, I took the phone to a local metal show where Gaerea and Conjurer were dimly lit in a dingy old bar. Usually, the harsh flashing lights and rapid onstage movements make it near-impossible to get a good, clear shot of the stage, doubly so if you're shooting video. If you enjoy snapping a quick picture or a clip of your favorite musicians, you'll be pleased by how detailed and impressive the camera system is at capturing key details while retaining the atmosphere. It didn't matter if that meant harsh red lighting, a submersive blue hue, or a brief, bright flash of light; the results were eye-catching and true to life. I was just as impressed with what the 42MP front-facing selfie camera could do. I'm not someone who takes many photos, but I understand the importance of being seen and well-lit for videoconferencing, or just chatting with friends on platforms like Discord, Instagram, WhatsApp, or Facebook Messenger. With its powerful autofocus and wider field of view, I was confident in front of the camera, and it yielded far better results than when I took similar photos with my iPhone 15 Pro Max or with my fiancée's Samsung Galaxy S25; the two former flagships have 12MP shooters, and just can't compare the same way. I'm torn on the Google Pixel 11 Pro. I love the design, adore the cameras, and appreciate the full commitment to Gemini inside, but as a value package, it is challenging to wholeheartedly recommend the device, particularly given the fact that it's only marginally better than the Pixel 10 Pro, and that it falls behind many other four-digit flagships on the market in terms of raw performance potential. I'm not convinced this is a phone you should pay at least $1,099 / £1,079 / €1,199. That said, strong competition means the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL will get better prices in sales events if the price history of previous Pixels is anything to go by. I've already seen deals including $315 off the 11 Pro XL and $265 off the smaller 11 Pro, so it's worth keeping an eye out at Amazon if you're happy to buy the phone outright. Of course, the Pixel 10 Pro and Pro XL are still excellent phones, but stock seems to be really drying up already, and when I have seen them lately, the deal prices on the 11 Pro models have actually been lower. So if you want a really good deal on the older models, you'll be looking at refurbs/renewed only pretty soon. Should you want the latest from the Pixel ecosystem and you're accepting of the trade-offs for stronger AI integration and computational photography over raw performance power, then there's just about enough here to justify the Pixel 11 Pro if last year's model doesn't appeal to you. Pixels may no longer be the disruptive flagship killers they once were. Instead, the Pixel 11 Pro has confidently cemented a position as a viable third option. If you don't want to buy the latest iPhone and don't want the bloatware of Samsung's One UI or Galaxy ecosystem, then it's the device to consider instead. The handset lives in an awkward middle ground for enthusiasts who want one thing done exceptionally well. If you love on-device AI and all the benefits of computational photography, then it's the go-to; for everyone else, you may want to look toward a sub-four-digit device instead. By   	James Hibberd  Writer-at-Large  Sony Pictures and filmmaker Sam Mendes have been mulling some innovative ideas for the release of their four Beatles biopics — including lumping together the films’ box office returns.  	The first glimpse of their strategy came over the weekend when Mendes’ producing partner Pippa Harris pulled back the curtain a bit. “We want people to be able to experience them in the cinema at the same time, during the same period,” she said at the BFI London Film Festival’s Industry Forum keynote session. “Now that doesn’t necessarily mean we’re thinking that people will go and see all four films on the same day. But within the same month, you might see one a week, or you might see one film one weekend and another the next.”  	            	 	 		 					Related Stories		 	             	 	Movies 			    	 		 					Beatles Films Release Details: A Mega-Month of Moviegoing, Producers Hope		 			               	 	Movies 			    	 		 					Aaron Sorkin's 'The Social Reckoning': First Reactions		 			         	Harris’ comments have been interpreted a couple of different ways — such as the movies potentially being released on different weeks during the same month. But sources tell The Hollywood Reporter the director and the studio have long mulled dropping all four movies the same day.  	In addition, Mendes and the studio have been pondering a highly unique reporting structure for the films’ box office receipts. Instead of releasing each film’s tally individually, the studio has been considering lumping the returns of all four movies together.  	This would, in effect, prevent the expected horse-race drama of “the John Lennon movie is $12 million more popular than the George Harrison movie,” or whatnot. The ticket-sales-per-movie data would still likely get out into the media from independent sources, however.  	“Who’s your favorite Beatle?” has been a topic of conversation and debate that has followed the band since it was first formed, and there’s an understandable reluctance to have the Beatles films put an exact popularity ranking and dollar figure on that question — particularly since the two surviving Beatles, Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr, are actively involved in the films. The legendary musicians have provided feedback on the scripts and met with the respective actors playing their roles (Paul Mescal, Harris Dickinson, Joseph Quinn and Barry Keoghan play Paul, John, George and Ringo, respectively.)  	           	Another idea being considered is offering a four-pack of tickets to encourage fans to buy tickets to all the movies at once instead of cherry-picking one or two to watch in theaters and saving the rest for streaming. It’s not clear how this one would actually work in practice, however, as it would presumably involve getting the major cinema chains to implement an unusual ticket-buying structure.  	Assuming all four movies do indeed drop the same week, sources also say the plan is to market the films as not having a particular order — that there will be no “right” order in which to watch the films.  	Each of these fab four ideas points to Mendes and the studio looking for creative solutions to address the broader challenge of getting audiences to watch not just one movie about the Beatles, but a quartet, each told from the perspective of a different member of the band, without giving any one movie more weight or using a structure that pushes one film to potentially cannibalize the audience for another.  	Sources emphasize that these plans remain fluid amid ongoing discussions and could change.   	The Beatles movies open in April 2028, which Sony doubtless hopes will be a relatively competition-light spot on the calendar to ensure there’s enough space in each market for John, Paul, George and Ringo to get enough screens each. by Jason Lemkin | 5 Interesting Things, Blog Posts, Scale Since August it has paid 2.7x ARR for Airtable and 2.3x for Miro. That is $1.08 billion of ARR for $2.64 billion of enterprise value, signed 37 days apart. Its own stock trades at roughly 8x to 10x revenue with both deals included. A dollar of Airtable’s revenue is worth about four times as much inside Bending Spoons as it was to Airtable’s own shareholders. The company has been public for a little over 100 days. In that time it reported its first quarter, closed Airtable on September 4, and signed Miro on September 10. Moody’s and S&P both upgraded it, and on October 2 it closed another $1.25 billion and €395 million of term loans.  Last Friday, CEO Luca Ferrari told Bloomberg that falling software valuations are a buying opportunity and that AI now writes at least 90% of the company’s code. In August we wrote that Airtable’s 2.7x ARR was the market price. Five weeks later Miro sold to the same buyer at 2.3x. If you run a company at $300M to $800M in ARR growing under 25%, or sit on the board of one, this is the buyer that is at least likely to call.  Even if they only do a handful of deals a year in the end.  Less than 10. The Q2 numbers, reported August 13: Nearly all of the $393M in added revenue came from six acquisitions: AOL, Eventbrite, Harvest, MileIQ, Tractive, and Vimeo. Tractive and WeTransfer contributed the most organic growth. Remini and Splice declined. AOL, Eventbrite, and Vimeo together grew in the low single digits.  Ferrari said on the call that organic growth is an output of where the capital goes and that the company does not optimize for it. He will buy a business that is growing fast, growing slowly, flat, or occasionally shrinking, as long as the return clears the hurdle. The metric he compounds is earnings per share. Adjusted EPS grew 167% while the diluted share count grew 3%. Q2 revenue beat consensus, and adjusted EPS came in at $0.46 against a $0.27 estimate. The full-year revenue guide landed below the $2.9B consensus, and the stock fell 16% the next day, from $48.98 to $40.92. At about $38 the equity is worth roughly $24 billion. Add net debt, and my rough math puts enterprise value at 7x to 8x pro forma revenue with Airtable and Miro included. Bending Spoons paid 2.7x for Airtable, which was growing more than 20%, and 2.3x for Miro. In Q2, Bending Spoons spent $58M on R&D, $73M on sales and marketing, and $92M on G&A. That is 8.3%, 10.3%, and 13.1% of revenue. Total operating expenses were 32% of revenue, and that figure includes $50M of reorganization costs. HubSpot spent 43.6% of revenue on sales and marketing and 24.8% on R&D in the same quarter. Datadog spent 27.8% and 42.6%. Each puts about 70% of revenue into the two lines combined. Bending Spoons puts in 18.6%.  The core team is nearly 700 people, whom the company calls Spooners. Revenue per Spooner passed $4M on an annualized basis in Q2. Total headcount, including people who stay on at acquired businesses, is higher. About 60 Spooners worked on Vimeo in Q2, roughly the same number that worked on the Evernote transformation in 2023. Vimeo is about four times Evernote’s size by revenue and more complicated technically. The rest of the margin comes from reorganizations. Q2 carried $51M of reorganization expense, including separation packages at AOL, Eventbrite, Tractive, and Vimeo. At Tractive, the plan was to cut around 160 of roughly 300 jobs. Today we’re laying off a large part of the Airtable team. This is not a reflection of their work but a reflection of our deep belief that small teams ship more and better. For Airtable, better is about to look like:– A new Core team shipping your top requests monthly (already… — Federico Simionato (@fedesimio) October 12, 2026  Miro’s enterprise value is $1.355B, on about $600M of ARR, nearly 90% of it from business and enterprise customers. It serves more than 250,000 organizations, has nearly 4 million paying users, and has over 750 customers above $100K in ARR. It was valued at $17.5B in early 2022. Airtable went for $1.285B on about $480M of ARR. Together that is $1.08B of ARR for $2.64B of enterprise value, signed 37 days apart. The equity checks total about $4.0B, because the two companies held roughly $1.4B of net cash between them. Ferrari told analysts the company underwrites deals to a 25% unlevered IRR and a 65% levered IRR. At the portfolio’s 54% adjusted operating margin, a 25% return supports a price of about 2.2x ARR.  That is my arithmetic and their margin, applied to businesses they have not finished reorganizing. It still explains why two very different companies cleared within 0.4 turns of each other. Neither price moved much for Airtable’s faster growth or for Miro’s $17.5B last round. Ferrari also explained why enterprise B2B is in the buy box now. About half of revenue already comes from businesses. He said enterprise software was priced too high for a buyer who makes money from free cash flow, and that prices have become more reasonable. If valuations stay near these levels, he said, the company will probably do more of these deals. The target list from the IPO prospectus has more than 1,000 companies on it, with nearly $400B of combined 2025 revenue. Sellers were paid dollar for dollar for their cash and 2.3x to 2.7x for the business. Airtable’s roughly $965M of net cash was 43% of its equity value. On September 25, Bending Spoons priced a $1.25B add-on to its dollar term loan B, against a $750M target. A €395M add-on to the euro term loan B priced the same day, against a target of $250M equivalent. Both are due 2031. That week Moody’s upgraded the company to Ba3 from B1 and S&P to BB- from B+. The loans closed October 2. The stock closed at $33.07 on October 6, down 16% in a month and 44% below the August high.  Miro is funded with those term loans, plus $295M of newly issued shares that Miro’s selling shareholders agreed to take out of their proceeds. Bending Spoons sold no stock to the public at $33. Q2 interest expense was $109M, up from $36M a year earlier, on $4.88B of long-term debt. That is 45% of GAAP operating income, before any borrowing for Miro. $794M of that debt matures within twelve months of June 30. The 2.4x leverage ratio needs a careful read. The EBITDA in the denominator is pro forma for acquisitions. It credits reorganization savings as if they had been in place for the full twelve months, and it includes certain savings that are expected but not yet achieved. The stock ended the week about 31% above the IPO price and 35% below the high. Ferrari told Bloomberg that AI produces at least 90% of the company’s code and supports product design, monetization work, and candidate assessment. He declined to put a number on the savings. He said the payoff is in scaling the acquisition model and improving businesses faster. The Q2 release describes the internal tool behind that. Alt-Spooner is a personal agent that works with the same access as the employee it belongs to. It runs on open-weight models the company hosts itself and can be switched to any other model. It went to every Spooner in early July and processed more than 100 billion tokens in its first three weeks. Ferrari gave one example on the call. Evernote’s general manager asked the agent in Slack to check whether a bug had been reported by other customers, find the root cause, write the fix, and send the pull request to the tech lead. That took minutes. He estimated it previously took about a week. He was more cautious about what customers will pay. AI features are producing some uplift, but a customer paying 100 is willing to pay about 110. He said he has not seen a customer go from 100 to 200, and that none of the company’s strategies depend on that changing.  The one business where he sees possible AI damage is Remini, the AI photo app. Existing customers behave as before, but new ones became harder and more expensive to win as image generation commoditized.
